en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
*Abhidhānappadīpikā*: A Lamp for Designations;
Salutation to the Buddha.
The Tathāgata, who is the doer of compassion,
having set forth and not abandoned the path that bestows happiness,
performed for the welfare of others in a world arisen in the age of strife.
I pay homage to him who performed what is entirely difficult to do;
even the elephant-like sages, though advanced in age, offered worship to him through the homage of the Dhamma.
Where those free from pain and other afflictions have crossed over to the further shore,
where men and non-men stand firm—
cross that path of Dhamma which destroys the flood of suffering.
Homage to the Sangha!
Praise be to the Lord of Sages, who has transcended the state of being a son of Māra,
who is extolled as a supreme field of merit in the world, and who is heard of again and again.
Even a multitude is better when they have undertaken restraint,
being constantly and without interval filled with a flood of virtues.
This is the promise.
Skill in names and genders is the cause for determining the ultimate meaning;
therefore, O Buddha, it is of great power for one who desires proficiency in speech.
Thus, I shall explain the names and genders as spoken by the Buddha, which are worthy of being recited.
I shall demonstrate and elucidate the Abhidhānappadīpikā, [employing] further grammatical rules (paribhāsā),
other word forms (rūpantara), and in some instances, by way of usage (cariya).
In some cases, the gender—feminine, masculine, or neuter—is to be understood according to the specific rule.
For those words whose genders are not distinct, as well as for *dvanda* compounds, the gender is that of the word expressing the gender itself.
Others hold that in the case of the end or middle of a verse-quarter, the preceding word takes [the gender of the following], while the following word takes [the gender of the preceding].
The particle *tu* occurs after a masculine or feminine noun in two cases, and after nouns of all genders in three cases;
it is to be known as occurring at the beginning of a subsequent term in the Abhidhamma, as well as at the end of a word, and so forth.
Furthermore, depending on usage, it appears in certain places within the Buddhist scriptures (*Āgama*).
Having mastered the *Nighaṇḍu* and its logic, the names and genders are now explained.
1. Section on Heaven:
The Buddha, the Ten-Powered One, the Teacher, the Omniscient, the Supreme among Humans;
The Sage of the Munis, the Blessed One, the Protector, the Visionary, the Aṅgīrasa, the Silent One;
the Lord of the World, the Supreme among Men, the Great Seer, the Guide;
the All-Seeing, the Well-Gone, the One of Vast Wisdom, and the Conqueror of Māra.
The lion among men, the best of men, the King of Dharma, the Great Sage;
the God of gods, the Honored One of the world, the Lord of Dharma, the Tathāgata.
The Self-Existent, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the Leader of supreme wisdom.
The Victor, Siddhattha, Sakka, Suddhodana, Gotama, the Lion of the Śākyas,
the Śākya, the Sage, and the Kinsman of the Sun;
liberation, cessation, Nibbāna, the island, the supreme destruction of craving.
It is the protection, the shelter, and the island for those in the wilderness; it is the peaceful, true, and unattached state.
It is the unconditioned, auspicious, and selfless, exceedingly difficult to see;
it is the supreme goal, the refuge, and likewise the freedom from distress.
The taintless, stable, and invisible has been realized;
it is disintegrated, subtle, infinite, and imperishable.
It is the destruction of suffering, freedom from affliction, the turning away from distress, the secure, and the absolute.
Apavagga and virāga, the sublime state beyond death;
yogakkhema, the further shore, liberation, peace, and purification;
the unconditioned element of deliverance, purity, and extinction—these may be [synonyms].
One whose taints are destroyed is a *asekha*, as is one free from passion,
an *arahant*; the world of the gods, heaven, bliss, the firmament, the triple heaven,
and the abode of the thirty-three.
The Tidasa, the Amara, the Deva, the Vibudha, and the Sudhāsina;
the Suras, the Marus, the Divokas, the Matapas, and the Saggavāsins;
the Nijjaras, the Animisas, the Dibbas, the Apumes, and the Devatās—these are indeed devatās, for the suffix is used here in its own sense (according to the Ṭīkā).
Siddhas, bhūtas, gandhabbas, guhyakas, yakkhas, rakkhasas, kumbhaṇḍas, pisācas, and so forth, are specified as divine births.
The pubbadevas and suraripus are asuras; the terms dānava and asura are masculine.
His other sons were Pahārāda, Saṃbara, Bali, and others.
His grandfather was Brahmā, the Lord of the World, who sits upon a lotus;
likewise Hiraññagabbha and Pajāpati, the eldest of the gods.
Vāsudeva is Hari, Hara (the Ṭīkā says Kaṇha), Keśava, and Cakrapāṇi;
Mahīśvara is Śiva, the wielder of the trident, the Lord, and also Paśupati.
Hara is said to be Kumāra, while Khaṇḍa shall be the bearer of the spear.
Sakka, the first-giver, the god, the king who wields the thunderbolt;
the lord of Sujā, the thousand-eyed one, Mahinda, armed with the vajra;
Vāsava, the thousand-eyed one, the ruler of the three heavens.
Suranātha, Vajira, Hattha, and Bhūtapatī;
Maghavā, Kosiya, Indra, Vatrabbhu, and Pākasāsana;
Vidhōja, then Sujā—his wife was Sujātā—and his city was Pura.
Masakkasāra, Masakkasāra (Sī.), Vassoka, Sārā, and Amarāvatī;
the Vejayanta palace,
and the Sudhammā assembly hall is thus considered.
His chariot is the Vejayanta,
Mātali is said to be his charioteer;
Erāvaṇa is his pale elephant, and Kambala is his stone throne.
Suvīra and others are the sons; Nandā is the lotus pond;
Nandana, Missaka, Citta, Latā, and Phārusaka are the groves.
Asani and dvi-kulisa are masculine; vajira is neuter.
The celestial nymphs mentioned are Accharā, Yojanā, Rambhā, Alambusā, and others;
the Gandhabba women include Pañcasikhā and others.
A celestial mansion is called a vimāna or byamha; nectar is amata or sudhā.
Sineru, Meru, Tidiva, Dhāra, Neru, and Sumeru;
Yugandhara, Īsadhara, Karavīka, Sudassana;
Nemindhara, Vinataka, Assakaṇṇa—these are the mountain ranges.
Likewise, there are the Mandākinī and the Ākāsa; then the Gaṅgā, the river of the gods;
the Koviḷāra and the Pāricchattaka, the Pārijātaka;
and the Kapparukkha and the Santāna—these would be the divine trees of the gods.
Pācī, patījhu, dīcī, itthī, pubba, pacchima, uttarā—these are the directions;
then dakkhiṇā is the south, pācī is the east, and there would be the intermediate directions (vidisā) and the sub-directions (anudisā).
Erāvata and Erāvaṇa (the latter in the Sīhaḷa recension), while in the Amarakosa only Erāvata exists; [and] Puṇḍarīka, Vāmana, Kumuda, and Añjana.
Pupphadanta is the lord of all lands; Suppatīka is the elephant of the [northeastern] direction.
Dhatarattha is the lord of the Gandhabbas, while Viruḷhaka and Virūpakkha are proclaimed as the lords of the Kumbhaṇḍas and the Nāgas, respectively.
Vessavaṇa, Kuvera, the lord of yakkhas, has men as his vehicle;
Alakā—also known as Alakamandā—is his city, and his weapon is the mace.
These are, in order, the lords of the four quarters, beginning with the East.
Jātaveda, Sikhī, Joti, Pāvaka, Dahana, Anala;
Hutāvaha, Accimā, Dhūma, Ketu, Aggi, Gini, Bhānumā;
Tejo, Dhūmasikha, Vāyu-sakha, and Kaṇhavattanī.
*Vessānara*, *hutāsa*, *tha*, *sikhājāla*, *acci*, and *cāpu* [mean fire]. *Vipphuliṅga* and *phuliṅga* mean sparks.
*Bhasma* and *abhasma*—these two words are included in the *rājādi* group (*Rūpasiddhi-uṇādi*); however, according to the *Sīhaḷaṭṭhakathā*, *bhasma* means ashes or chaff.
*Kukkuḷa* refers to hot ashes. *Maṅgāra*, *alāta*, and *mummuka*—this triad refers to glowing wood as fuel (*Ṭīkā*).
The fuel-stick, the kindling wood, and likewise the tinder and the firewood;
as well as the light and the illumination—
these are all equal to the world, the radiance, and the heat.
Māluta, pavana, vāyu, vāta, anila, samīraṇa, gandhavāha,
as well as vāyo, samīra, and sadāgati—
these are the sixteen divisions of wind: upward-moving and downward-moving.
The belly is the receptacle, following the course of the inhalation;
furthermore, the out-breath is the exhalation,
while the inhalation is released as *āna*.
Vega, java, raya, khippaṃ, tu, sīghaṃ, turitaṃ, lahu;
āsu, tuṇṇa, maraṃ, and also lambitaṃ and tuvaṭaṃ.
Satataṃ, niccaṃ, avirata, nārata, santata, anavirataṃ, and dhruvaṃ.
*Bhusa*, *matisayo*, and *daḷhaṃ*; *tibba*, *ikanta*, and *atimatta* mean "intense"; *bāḷhāni* means "strong.
*Khippa* and so forth [mean] "quick" and apply to things (*dabbe*) that are neuter (*paṇḍaka*); those which are in the three [genders] are feminine (*dabbagā*).
*Aviggaha*, however, is *kāma*; it may also be *manobhū* and *madana*.
Antaka, Vasavattī, Pāpimā, and Pajāpati;
Kaṇha, the kinsman of the heedless, Māra, and Namuci—these are his names.
His daughters are Taṇhā, Aratī, and Ragā; his elephant is Girimekhala.
Yama the King is the wind, and Yama is his weapon, the eye;
Vepacitti and Puloma, the Kimpurisa and the Kinnara.
The atmosphere, the sky, the sun, the path, the cloud, the firmament, and the ether.
Vehāsa, anilapatha, ākāsa, nitthiya, and nabha are synonyms for the sky.
Deva, vehāyasa, tāra, patha, surapatha,
and agha are synonyms for the celestial realm.
Megha, valāhaka, deva, pajjunna, ambudhara, ghana;
dhārādhara, jīmūta, vārivāha, and likewise ambuda.
Abbha and then tīsa, vassa, vassana, and vuṭṭhi are feminine.
A flash of lightning is called *sateratā* or *akkhaṇā*; lightning is also known as *vijjutā* or *acirappabhā*.
The deep sound of thunder is termed *dhanitaṃ*, *gajjitaṃ*, *rasitā*, and so forth.
A rainbow is the *indāvudha* or *indadhanu*; a spray of water tossed by the wind is *sīkara*.
A shower is a falling stream of rain;
hailstones, however, are raindrops like stones from a cloud.
A cloudy day is one covered by clouds; a lid, moreover, is a covering.
Tirodhāna, antaradhāna, pidhāna, and chādana;
indu, canda, and nakkhattarāja;
soma, nisākara, osadhīsa, himaraṃsi, sasaṅka, candimā, and sasī.
*Sītaraṃsi*, *nisānātha*, and *uḷurāja* are masculine terms for "moon.
A sixteenth part [of the moon] is called a *kalā*. The *bimba* is the orb (*maṇḍala*);
the *aḍḍha*, *addha*, and *upaḍḍha* may also mean a half, or else they refer to a portion (*khaṇḍa*) as a masculine noun.
*Addhaṃ* is said to mean a half or an equal portion; *pasāda*, however, means clarity or serenity.
*Komudī*, *candikā*, and *juṇhā* refer to moonlight. *Kanti*, *sobhā*, *juti*, and *chavi* denote radiance, beauty, brilliance, and luster.
*Kalaṅka*, *lañchana*, *lakkhaṃ*, *aṅka*, *abhiññāṇa*, and *lakkhaṇa* signify a stain, a mark, a spot, a sign, a token, and a characteristic.
Cihanaṃ and sobhā denote beauty, while susama signifies supreme equanimity.
Sīta refers to coldness; these words take the gender of the quality they describe (guṇiliṅga). Sīta, sisira, and sītalā mean cold;
hima, tuhina, and mussāva denote frost; and nīhāra and mahikā likewise refer to mist or snow.
Nakkhatta, Joti, Bhaṃ, and Tārā; Apuma, Tāraka, and Aḷu;
Assayuja, Bharaṇī, Itthī, Saka, Attikā, Rohiṇī, and Pica;
Migasira, Maddā, and Punabbasu; Phusso, Pusso, and Āsilesa.
Māghā, Maghā, and Phagguṇī; Hatthā, Cittā, and Svāti;
Visākhā, Anurādhā, and Jeṭṭhā; Mūlā, and the two Āsāḷhās;
Savaṇa, Dhaniṭṭhā, Satabhiṣaj, and the Pūrva- and Uttara-Bhaddapadas.
Including Revatī as well, there are twenty-seven constellations in order.
Rāhu is said to be Sobhaṇa; the nine planets are the Sun and the rest.
The zodiac signs begin with Aries (Meṣa); the auspicious quarters are equal to those of the *poṭṭhapada*.
Ādicca, Suriya, Sūra, Sataraṃsi, Divākara;
Verocana, Dinakara, Uṇharaṃsi, Pabhaṅkara;
Aṃsumālī, Dinapati, Tapana, Ravi, Bhānumā.
Raṃsimā, bhākara, bhānu, akka, and sahassaraṃsi are synonyms for the sun.
Raṃsi, ābhā, pabhā, ditti, ruci, bhā, jutī, dīdhiti, marīci, dvīsu, bhānu, aṃsu,
mayūkha, kiraṇa, and kara are synonyms for a ray of light.
*Paridhi*, *pariveso*, *tha*, *marīci*, *migataṇhikā*;
that which exists before the rising of the sun is called *aruṇa*.
*Kālo*, *addhā*, *samayo*, *velā*.
The remaining terms,
such as *khaṇa* and so forth, are as follows:
ten *khaṇas* constitute a *laya*, and ten *khaṇas* would be a *lava*.
Ten layas make a khaṇalaya;
ten of those make a muhutta;
ten khaṇamuhuttas make a day, and ten days make a dina.
Pabhāta, vibhāta, paccūsa, and kalla;
abhidoso, padoso, sāya,
sañjhā, and dinaccaya.
*Nisā*, *rajanī*, *ratti*, *tiyāmā*, and *saṃvarī* are synonyms for night.
When joined with the moon, it is *juṇhā* (*candikāyuttā*); when thick with darkness, it is *timisikā*.
*Nisītha* is the middle watch of the night, while *aḍḍharatta* is the great midnight.
Andhakāra, tama, and nitthīna are synonyms for darkness; timisa and timira are also considered such.
Likewise, caturaṅgatama refers to the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.
A dense mass of clouds is called vanasaṇḍa, and a film of mist is called paṭala, as is the middle of the night.
*Andhatamaṃ* means thick darkness; *pahāra* means watch (*yāma*); it is known as *saññita*.
The first day is *pāṭipada*, the second is *dutiyā*, and so on for the third and subsequent days. A *tithi* is so called because it "protects" or "preserves" (*tāyati pāleti*);
[the suffix] *-i* is added according to the rule beginning with *ṇvu* (Pāṇini 3.1.134). *Paṇṇarasī* is *pañcadasī*; *puṇṇamāsī* is *puṇṇamā*.
The new moon is *amāvasī*, and the fifteenth day is the full moon (*pannāsī*). Sixty *ghaṭikā*s make one *horā* (day and night);
fifteen of those make a fortnight (*pakkha*). These two, the preceding and the following, are the bright and dark [fortnights].
Kāḷā, Māsa, and Tuvaṭṭa;
Citta, Vesākha, and Jeṭṭha; Sāḷha, followed by two Sāvaṇas;
Poṭṭhapāda and Assayuja; and the twelve months ending with Kattika.
Māgasira, then Phussa, followed by Māgha and Phagguṇa;
the months of Kattika and Assayuja, and Pacchimakattika and Pubbakattika;
Sāvaṇa is the month of departure.
But the delightful Cittamāsa consists of four months each, starting from the dark fortnight of Kattika;
these are respectively the seasons of winter, summer, and the rains, occurring in pairs.
Hemanta, sisira, and mutū,
then vassa, gimha, and vassāna; and sarada—
these are the seasons, with two months each as stated in due order.
The hot season, the scorching heat, and summer;
the rainy season, the rains,
and the pouring clouds— these three seasons of the year, along with the winter months, constitute the sun's southern course.
Consider the *uttarāyaṇa* (northern course), the two [periods] of the rainy season (*vassāyana*), and the three [periods];
the *vassa*, *saṃvacchara*, *nitthī*, *sarada*, *hāyana*, and *samā* are synonyms for year.
Furthermore, *kappakkhaya*, *saṃvaṭṭa*, *yuganta*, and *palaya* refer to the end of an eon.
*Alakkhī* is an ill-fated woman; *lakkhī*, on the other hand, refers to a woman of fortune (*siri*).
*Danu* is the mother of the Dānavas; *aditi* is the mother of the gods.
*Pāpa*, *kibbisa*, and *vera* mean evil; *gha* means misconduct (*duccarita*) and misdeed (*dukkaṭa*).
That which is non-meritorious, unwholesome, dark, turbid, and evil is called *apuñña*, *akusala*, *kaṇha*, *kalusa*, *durita*, and *agu*. That which is wholesome,
well-performed, bright, meritorious, and the Dhamma praised by the wise is called *kusala*,
*sukata*, *sukka*, *puñña*, *dhamma*, *manitthiya*, *sucarita*, *addha*, *dhammika*, and *ihalokika*.
The visible is this world, and the beyond is the world hereafter;
"at that time" refers to the present,
while "subsequent time" refers to the future.
Laughter, exultation, rapture, feeling, and joy in women;
bliss, gladness, delight, contentment, jubilation, and intoxication;
and then joy, gladness, happiness, pleasure, and comfort.
*Bhadda*, *seyyo*, *subha*, *khema*, *kalyāṇa*, *maṅgala*, and *siva* [denote] the auspicious.
*Dukkha*, *kasira*, *kiccha*, *nīgha*, *byasana*, and *agha* [denote] suffering.
In the case of material things (*dabbe*), however, they denote evil and merit; in the case of the three [times], they denote lack of difficulty, happiness, and so forth.
Fortune, destiny, lot, and portion; what is ordained by fate;
furthermore, arising, manifestation, birth, procreation, and origin.
Sign, cause, ground, basis, seed, and bond.
*Nidāna*, *pabhava*, *hetu*, *sambhava*, *setu*, and *paccaya* are synonyms.
That which is the immediate cause is considered the *padatthāna* (proximate cause).
Furthermore, *jīva*, *purisa*, *atta*, and *thā* are used as primary terms for the natural state (*pakati*).
A living being, a physical body, an element, a creature, an embodied one, and a person;
a soul, a breath, progeny, a creature,
a person, the world, and likewise the Tathāgata.
Form, sound, odor, taste, contact, and mental objects are the spheres of experience;
they are the six supports, the domains, the delightful, the objects, and the focal points.
White, fair, bright, and pure.
Dhavala means white or pale;
soṇa, however, means red or crimson;
tamba, mañjiṭṭha, and rohitā mean tawny or madder-red.
Blue, black, dark, and dark-blue;
mottled, grey, and deep-dark grey;
white and yellow are called pale, while slightly pale is called dusty-grey.
For a short while, it was dawn-colored,
pale red, and crimson; then it was yellow,
with the luster of turmeric.
Palāsa is green or yellow.
Kaḷāra is brownish-yellow or blue; when yellow, it has the luster of gorocana.
Piṅga or pisaṅga, or alternatively, kaḷāra and the others, refer to tawny-brown.
*Kammāsa*, *sabala*, and *citta* [denote] variegation;
*sāva*, however, [denotes] blackish-yellow.
These [words] agree with the gender of the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*), whereas *sukka* and so forth, when denoting the quality itself, are masculine.
Dancing (*naccam*), acting (*naṭṭam*), dancing (*naṭanam*), acting (*nattanam*), and the art of dance (*lāsanam*) are its synonyms.
Dancing (*naccam*), instrumental music (*vādita*), and song (*gītam*)—this triad constitutes the dramatic performance (*nāṭum*).
The place for dancing may be the stage (*raṅgo*); acting (*bhinayo*) is the indication by means of gestures (*sūcyasūcanam*).
Aṅgahāra is the movement of the limbs; naṭṭaka, naṭaka, and naṭa are actors.
The erotic, the pathetic, the heroic, the wondrous, the comic, the terrifying, the peaceful, the loathsome, and the furious—these are the nine dramatic sentiments (nāṭyarasa).
When a man desires a woman and a woman desires a man,
that longing which is the cause of sexual play and the like is called *śṛṅgāra* (the erotic sentiment).
It is the most excellent mode of expression, having as its basis men and women.
Thus, union and separation are considered the two types of the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra).
Speech is spoken of as utterance, expression, discourse, communication, word, and speech.
*Utti*, *vācā*, *girā*, *vāṇī*, *bhāratī*, and *kathā*—these are said to be synonyms for speech (*vacī*).
A collection of words consisting of a single expression may be called a sentence (*vākya*) when it possesses a verb (*sakāraka*).
"Repetition" (*āmeḍita*) should be understood as uttering [the same word] two or three times.
A wise person should employ repetition (*āmeḍita*) in cases of fear, anger, praise, haste, curiosity, envy, laughter, sorrow, and faith. *Iru*, *nārī*,
*yaju*, and *sāma*— these would be the three Vedas, beginning with *miti*.
These very three are the woman, the Veda, the mantra,
and the well-frequented ford. Aṭṭhaka, Vāmaka, Vāma, Devala,
Caṅgīrasa, Bhagu, Yamadaggi, Vāsiṭṭha, Bhāradvāja, and Kassapa.
Vessāmitta— these are the seers who were the authors of the mantras.
Kappa, Vyākaraṇa, Joti, Sutta, Sikkhā, and Nirutti,
along with Chandoviciti— these they call the six Vedāṅgas.
Itihāsa is what has occurred in the past, such as the compositions beginning with the Mahābhārata.
A treatise that makes names known is a nighaṇḍu, such as those concerning trees and other things.
That which is called Lokāyata should be understood as the treatise of caviling (vitaṇḍasattha).
The *Keṭubha* is the ritual procedure (*kriyākappa*), while the *Vikappa* is beneficial for poets.
The *Ākhyāyikā* is a narrative based on actual events, and the *Kathā* is the composition of a plot.
In the science of ethics (*arthasattha*), *Daṇḍanīti* refers to both the legal code and the account of historical occurrences.
Saññā, khya, vha, samaññā, abhidhāna, and nāma are synonyms;
nāmadheyya, adhivacana, and paṭivākya are further terms for it.
Pañha, anuyoga, pucchā, and nidassana are likewise synonyms.
Upagghāta, diṭṭhanta, and likewise udāharaṇa;
samā, saṅkhepa, saṃhāra, samāsa, and also saṅgaha;
and [the verse] beginning with "Sataṃ dhārayasi" are examples of empty speech (abbhakkhāna).
Vohāra means dispute (vivāda) or legal case; sapanā also means an oath (sapatha).
Yasa, siloka, and kitti mean fame;
ghosanā, however, means a loud noise.
*Paṭighoso* and *paṭiravo* mean echo or resonance; *paññāsa* refers to the mouth of speech.
*Katthanā*, *silāghā*, *vaṇṇanā*, *nuti*, and *tthuti* denote praise.
*Thomana* and *thomanaṃ* (in some places *thomanaṃ* and *thomanā* appear as two genders), as well as *pasaṃsā*, signify eulogy; *kekā* is the cry of the peacock (*sikhaṇḍin*).
The cry of elephants is *koñcanāda*;
the neighing of horses is *hesā*.
*Pariyāya* and *vevacana* are synonyms; *sākacchā* and *saṃkathā* mean conversation.
*Upavāda*, *upakkosa*, *vaṇṇavāda*, and *anuvāda*;
*janavāda*, *apavāda*, and *parivāda* are synonymous.
*Khepa*, *nindā*, *kucchā*, *jigucchā*, and *garahā* are likewise [synonyms].
Reproach preceded by censure is called "reviling.
That speech which proceeds by way of an improper and ignoble expression may be termed "abusive speech," as it indicates a transgression.
Muhubhāsā is idle chatter, while palāpa is speech that is empty;
ādabhāsana is conversation,
whereas vilāpa is lamentation.
"Vippalāpa" means contradiction; "sandesa," however, refers to verbal communication.
"Sambhāsana" is conversation, which is mutual discourse free from contradiction.
"Pharusa" is harsh speech; "manuñña" is speech that is pleasing and heart-touching.
That which is crowded and defiled, contradictory in its preceding and following parts, and devoid of collective meaning is designated as "abaddha" (unstrung);
furthermore, "vitatha" means false, and "āhata" means struck by falsehood (in some versions of the Amarakosa). The words beginning with "pharusa" (harsh) possess all three genders.
Right (sammā), false (vitatha), true (sacca), real (taccha), and according to fact (yathātatha);
their opposites are wrong (micchā) and untrue (musā). In the three worlds, these are called right and wrong.
Sound (ravo), resonance (ninādo), and noise (saddo).
Nigghosa, nāda, dhanaya, and rāva;
ārāva, saṃrāva, virāva, and ghosa;
ravā, sutitthī, sara, and nissanā.
Lucid, sweet, intelligible, worth hearing, far-reaching, distinct, deep,
and resonant— such is the voice with its eight qualities.
For the cry of those who have gone to the animal realm is called mere braying.
Kolāhalo and kalahalo,
gītaṃ, gānaṃ, and gītikā.
There are seven notes (sara), three scales (gāma), and twenty-one modulations (mucchanā).
There are forty-nine such positions (in many cases); this is the circle of notes (*saramaṇḍala*).
The *usabha*, *dheva*, *cha*, *gandhāra*, *majjhima*, *pañcama*, and *nisāda*—these seven are declared to be the notes (*sara*).
The cows low for the bull, and the horses neigh for the stallion;
the peacocks cry for the sixth note, the gandhāras for the fifth, the cranes and the *majā* birds for the middle note (*madhyama*).
The *parapuṭṭha* birds and others sing the fifth (*pañcama*), and the elephants utter the *niṣāda*.
The village of Chajja and Majjhima,
and the three called Sādhāraṇa:
in each of these sārās, there are indeed three modes of tuning.
In many instances, there may likewise be those *tāna* [consonant] positions; seven, six, and seven are found.
Three, two, and four, and four respectively for the vowels;
three, two, and four—thus there would be twenty-two *suti*s.
In a higher tone, it is *tāra*; in a steady, sweet, and soft tone, it is *kala*;
in a deep tone, it is *manda*; furthermore, *tāra* and the others [are used] in three ways, while *kala* is used in the *kākalī* (whispering) register when subtle.
The equality of the action and so forth is *laya*.
The lute (*vīṇā*) has seven strings; it is called a *vallakī* when there are seven strings, and a *parivādinī* when it has many strings.
The bowl of the lute is the *pokkhara*.
The *upavīṇa* is indeed a lute (*veṭhaka*).
Musical instruments are declared to be fivefold: the *ātata*, the *vitata*, the *mātatavitata*, the *ghana*, and the *susira*.
These constitute the five-membered orchestra (*pañcaṅgika*).
That which is called *ātata* consists of skins alone, such as drums (*bherī*) and the like,
when stretched over a single surface, including the *kumbha*, *thuṇa*, *daddarika*, and so forth.
That which is *vitata* has both surfaces stretched, such as musical instruments like the *muraja* drum and the like.
All that is stretched and stretched-out, such as the covered drum (paṇava) and so forth;
the hollow, such as the flute and conch; the solid, such as the cymbal and so forth;
and that which is struck to produce sound—this is called "instrumental music" (vādita), which is said to be "percussive" (vajja).
The *bherī* is called the *dundubhī*;
the *mudiṅga* is that of the *muraja*.
The *āliṅga*, *ṅkya*, and *ddhakā* are its varieties.
The *tiṇava* and the *ḍiṇḍima* are [types of drums];
the *ālambara* is the *paṇava*. The *koṇa* is the instrument for playing the lute and so forth.
The *daddarī*, the *paṭaha*, and the *bherī* are varieties of the *maddala* and others.
When the world is crushed by passion, there may arise a sweet fragrance;
yet that joy of yours is far-reaching, extending beyond the three worlds.
It is a desirable scent, fragrant, well-scented, and sweet-smelling.
"Pūtigandhi" means foul-smelling; "vissa" refers to that which has the smell of raw flesh.
Saffron, jasmine, tagara, and turukka—these are declared to be the four types of fragrant substances.
Astringent, bitter, sweet, salty, sour, and pungent—these are the six tastes; they are included within three [categories].
Contact may be called "contact" (phassa) or "the tangible" (phoṭṭhabba).
The sense organ that perceives objects is the skin and the eye;
it is also called the eye (*nayana*), the organ of sight (*netta*), the beholder (*locana*), the socket (*acchi*), and the eye-ball (*cakkhu*).
The ear is the apprehender of sound; it is the hearing (*savana*) and the auditory faculty (*sutī*); while *natthu* refers to the nose.
The nose is called *nāsā*, *nāsikā*, and *ghāna*; the tongue is *rasanā*.
The body is *sarīra*, *vapu*, *gatta*, *attabhāva*, *bondi*, and *viggaha*;
it is also *deha*, *kāya* (in the masculine), *tanu*, and *kaḷevara* (in the feminine).
Citta, ceto, mano, and nitthī; viññāṇa, hadaya, and likewise;
mānasa, dhī, and paññā; buddhi, medhā, mati, muti;
bhūrī, mantā, and paññāṇa; ñāṇa, vijjā, and yoni.
"Paṭibhāna" is non-delusion; "tha" refers to the divisions of wisdom and insight.
"Sammādiṭṭhi" and so forth refer to investigation; "vīmaṃsā," however, is analytical inquiry.
"Sampajañña" is discernment; "vedayita," however, is feeling.
Reasoning (takka), initial application (vitakka), and intention (saṅkappa);
breath (ppāṇa), inhalation (assāsa), and life (jīvita);
one-pointedness (ekaggatā), serenity (samatha), and non-distraction (avikkhepa) are concentration (samādhi).
Exertion, application, and striving, as well as effort and perseverance;
endeavor, energy, and zeal, as well as exertion and fortitude—
these are the four factors of energy, [applied] to the skin and the sinews.
The remaining of what was once whole, the withering away of flesh and blood;
Exertion is the striving of one who is resolute, mindfulness is the non-forgetfulness of one who is mindful;
Shame is the sense of modesty regarding what is equal, while dread of wrongdoing is the fear of evil.
Equanimity and neutrality, however, are neither-painful-nor-pleasant;
mental engagement is attention,
while resolution is decisiveness.
Compassion, pity, tenderness, and mercy;
kindness, non-cruelty, and likewise restraint from harm, as well as abstinence and delight [in virtue].
Forbearance, patience, enduring, and tolerance; and loving-kindness, as well as benevolence.
Vision is view (*diṭṭhi*), it is a conviction (*laddhi*); it may be a tenet (*siddhanta*) or a doctrine (*samaya*).
Craving (*taṇhā*) is thirst (*tasiṇā*), it is a goad (*ejā*); it is ensnaring (*jālinī*) and clinging (*visattikā*);
it is desire (*chanda*), a tangle (*jaṭā*), attachment (*nikanti*), and it is a seamstress (*sibbinī*) and the guide to existence (*bhavanetti*).
Covetousness is a forest, a snare, greed, lust, and attachment;
it is longing, desire, wish, yearning, and craving;
it is called aspiration and preference, while excessive longing is said to exist in two ways.
Enmity, hostility, malice, hatred, and resentment;
anger, ill-will, wrath, and rage—
these are malevolence and dissatisfaction.
A poultice is *baddhavera*; sorrow (*soka*) is the state of grieving;
weeping, wailing, and lamenting are *parideva* and *pariddava*.
Fear is *bhīti*, *itthi*, or *muttāsa*; terror is *bherava*, the great fear.
Bheravaṃ, bhīsanaṃ, bhīmaṃ, dāruṇaṃ, ca bhayānakaṃ;
ghoraṃ, paṭibhayaṃ, bhesmaṃ, bhayaṅkara—these [terms] are used in three genders.
Issā, usūyā, maccheraṃ, and also macchariya, maccharaṃ.
Delusion, ignorance, and likewise lack of knowledge; conceit, discrimination, and loftiness;
restlessness, agitation, and then "the mind runs upward by means of this," thus it is called *uddhava* (as stated in the *Ṭīkā*);
burning, remorse, and indeed regret; repentance, non-repentance, and *vippaṭisāra* are thus explained.
Manovilekha, sandeha, and saṃsaya are synonyms for kathaṃkathā;
dveḷhaka, vicikicchā, kaṅkhā, saṅkā, and vimati are also used.
Gabbha, bhimāna, and ahaṃkāra are synonyms, while cintā is said to be jhāna.
*Nicchaya* is said to be certainty (*niṇṇaya*); *paṭiññā*, however, is assent (*paṭissava*).
*Avamāna* is contempt (*tirakkāra*); *paribhava* is also disrespect (*anādara*).
*Parābhava* is humiliation (*avaññā*); *ummāda* is the derangement of the mind (*cittavibbhamo*).
*Pema*, *sineha*, and *sneha* mean affection; *cittapīḷā* and *visaññitā* mean mental distress;
*pamāda* and *sativossagga* mean negligence; *kotūhala* and *kutūhala* mean curiosity;
*vilāsa*, *lalita*, and *līlā* mean grace; *hāva*, *heḷā*, and *vibbhama* mean coquetry.
A woman may possess such qualities as these, which are actions born of the sentiment of the erotic (śṛṅgāra-rasa).
Laughter is *hasita*, *hāsa*; when it is mild, it is *mihita* or *sita*.
When it is loud, it is *aṭṭahāsa* or *mahāhāsa*.
Horripilation is *romañco*.
Joking, laughter, play, sport, amusement, and diversion are synonyms for *kīḷitaṃ*.
Sleep, dreaming, slumber, torpor, and drowsiness are synonyms for *niddā*.
Deceit, fraud, and cheating; hypocrisy, guile, and trickery;
while nature, release, essential form, and natural state [are synonyms for *sabhāva*].
Character, characteristic, and disposition [are synonyms for *sīla*].
A festival, a joy, and a celebration are considered synonymous (Ṭī.).

A person who bears this *Abhidhānappadīpikā* with affection perceives, according to their pleasure, the various meanings of the Minor Collection (*Khuddaka*) and other such works (variant: "the various meanings found in the Minor Collection and elsewhere").
The Section on Heaven is finished.
2. The Section on Beings. 1. The Chapter on the Grounds.
By means of *vagga*, *bhūmi*, *purī*, *macca*, *catubbaṇṇa*, *vana*, and so forth, as well as by *pātāla*, they are spoken of here [in this context];
likewise, through their various components (*apaṅga*), the term *saṅga* is used.
*Vasundharā*, *chamā*, *bhūmi*, *pathavī*, *medanī*, and *mahī* [are synonyms for earth].
Ubbī, vasumatī, gokkha, vasudhā, dharaṇī, dharā, puthavī, jagatī, bhūrī, bhū, bhūtadharā, and avanī are synonyms for the earth. Khārā, however, refers to clay;
ūso, ūsavā, and tūsaro refer to three types of saline soil.
Thalaṃ (the dry land) refers to the female gender for the earth’s surface, while jaṅgala refers to that which is hard and barren.
There are these four great continents: Pūrvavideha, Aparagoyāna, Jambudvīpa, and Uttarakuru.
The Kurus, Sakyas, Kosalas, Magadhas, Sivis, Kalingas, Avantis,
Pancalas, Vajjis, Gandharas, Cetis, Vangas, Videhas, Kambojas, Maddas,
Bhaggas, Angas, and Sinhalese— these many peoples are capable [of being ruled].
Kasmīra, Kāsi, Paṇḍava, and so forth, may be other countries.
"Loka" and "bhuvana" are said to mean the world; furthermore, "desa" and "visaya" mean a district.
"Milakkhadesa" means a borderland, while "majjhadesa" means the Middle Country.
*Anūpa* means rich in water; *kaccha* is used for both masculine and neuter genders.
*Saddala* refers to a place green with grass, specifically new grass.
A region sustained by river waters and where crops grow from rain is [called *anūpa*].
O King, he who has the river as his mother,
and Mātika in due order; likewise the three lowlands,
the moon, the sun, and that which is called eternal.
A kingdom (*raṭṭha*) and a conquered territory (*vijita*); a man (*purisa*), a bridge (*setu*), and a boundary (*āliya*).
A border region (*upāntabhū*), a surrounding area (*parisara*); a herd (*goṭṭha*), a cow-pen (*gokula*), and a flock (*vaja*).
A road (*magga*), a path (*pantha*), a way (*patha*), a journey (*addhā*), as well as a direct route (*añjasa*) and a track (*vaṭuma*).
*Pajja*, *pajjā*... (as above), *yana* and *padavī*, *vattanī*, *paddhati*, *itthiyam*;
its divisions are *jaṅgha*, *sakaṭa*, and *magga*, and these are *mahaddhana*.
*Ekapadyā* and *ekapadikā*, while *kantāra* refers to that which is difficult to traverse.
*Paṭimagga* and *paṭipatha* mean a path; *addhāna* means a long or short journey.
*Suppatha* and *supantha* mean a good road; *uppatha* and *apatha* would mean a by-path.
Thirty-six atoms (*paramāṇu*) make one *ṇu*, and thirty-six of those [make one *aṇu*].
Thirty-six *tajjārīs* make one *rathareṇu*; thirty-six of those make one *likkhā*.
Seven *likkhās* make one *ūkā*, and seven of those make one *dhaññamāsa*.
Seven *dhaññamāsas* make two *aṅgulas*, and two of those would be one *vidatthi*.
There are seven of those *ratanas*; twenty of them make a *yaṭṭhi*. Twenty *yaṭṭhis* make a *sabhā*.
Four *gāvutas* make a *musabhā*. Eighty *musabhās* make a *yojana*.
Five hundred *dhanus* make a *kosa*. Four *ambaṇas* make a *karīsa*.
The interior measurement of the hands is twenty-eight [finger-breadths].
The Chapter on the Ground is finished.
2. The Section on Earth (Bhūkaṇḍa).
2. Puravagga:
*Pura*, *nagara*, *mithi*, or *vā*; *ṭhānīya*, *puṭabhedana*;
*thiyaṃ* (or *thiya*), *rājadhānī*, and *rājaṭhānī* (according to the Ṭīkā); and *khandhāvāra*—these are synonyms for a city.
Except for the branch cities, there is that which is the root city:
Benares, Sāvatthī, Vesālī, Mithilā, Alavi,
Kosambī, Ujjenī, Takkasilā, Campā, and Sāgala.
Susumāragira, Saṃsumāra-rāja, Gaha, and Kapilavatthu;
Sāketa, Mindapatha, Kkaṭṭha, and Pāṭaliputtaka;
Jetuttara, Saṅkassa, Kusinārā, and other cities.
A *racchā* is said to be a lane, as are a carriage road (*rathikā*) and a street (*vīthi*).
A *byūha* is an unpierced lane, whereas a pierced one is a path (*patha*) or a track (*addhi*).
A crossroads (*catukka*) is a square (*caccara*), while a junction (*sandhi*) is a place where four roads meet (*siṅghāṭaka*).
A rampart (*pākāra*) is a fence (*varaṇa*); furthermore, *udāpo* and *uddāpa* mean a moat (*upakārikā*).
A wall (*kuṭṭa*) is a partition (*bhitti*); *nārī* means a woman. A gate-tower (*gopura*) is a gate-fortress (*dvārakoṭṭhaka*).
A pillar (*esikā*) is an *indakhīla*. A watchtower (*aṭṭa*) would be a turret (*aṭṭālaka*).
A *toraṇa* is an outer gate; a *parikhā* is a moat, and a *dīghikā* is a long pond.
A *mandira*, *sadaṇa*, *gāra*, *nikāya*, *nilaya*, and *laya* are synonyms for a dwelling.
An *āvāsa*, *bhavana*, *vesma*, *niketana*, and *nivesana* are also terms for a residence.
House, home, dwelling, refuge, shelter; abode, hall, ruin, residence;
woman’s quarters, hut, and also dwelling; house, and for a man, a mansion;
shrines, however, are the places of restraint.
The palace itself is the sacrificial post, and the roof is the turret;
the elephant’s forehead-bump is the post, while its trunk-tip is established as the base.
The curved roof is like a garuḍa, and there may be a half-yoke upon it.
A multi-storied building (māḷa) joined with a single pinnacle, or a square palace (pāsāda);
likewise, an assembly hall (sabhā), or a pavilion (maṇḍapa) which is a gathering place for people.
Furthermore, there was the assembly hall,
the place for walking meditation frequented by the Victor, his dwelling place, and also the fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭi);
then there was the kitchen where food was prepared, and the site of the great refectory.
*Āvesana* is a workshop or craft-hall; *soṇḍā* is a tavern.
*Vaccaṭṭhāna* is a latrine or privy; the dwelling place of sages is called *assama*.
A shop for selling merchandise is *kuṭi*; *āpaṇa* is a market stall or marketplace.
An *udositam* is a storehouse; a *caṅkamanam*, however, is a walking path.
A *jantāgharam* is a sauna; a *papā* is a water-shed.
A *gabbho* is a chamber or dwelling; a *gāram*, however, is a bedchamber.
The women’s quarters (*itthāgāra*), the harem (*orodha*), the pure precinct (*suddhanta*),

and the inner apartments (*anteura*)— these are considered the king’s private domain (*kacchantara*), a place where vulgar objects do not enter. A staircase (*sopāna*) or an ascent (*ārohaṇa*) [is also included].
A ladder, a staircase;
a window and a casement, and a lattice and a lion’s cage.
A light-shaft is mentioned there; a railing is for women, and a crossbar would be the paligha.
*Kapisīsa* (the head of the door), *ggalatthambha* (the pillar at the threshold), and *nibbaṃ* (the lintel) are [parts of] the *chaddakoṭi*.
*Chadana*, *paṭala*, and *chadda* mean a roof or covering. *Majira*, *caccara*, and *ṅgaṇa* mean a courtyard.
*Paghāna*, *paghanā*, *linda*, and *pamukha* refer to the porch or entrance-hall. *Dvārabandhana* means the door-bolt or fastening of the door.
The door is the *piṭṭhasaṅghāṭaka*; the lintel is the *bāhā*, while the threshold is the *kaṇṇikā*.
The door-bolt is the *paṭihāra*; the step is the *ummāra* (masculine). The wedge is the *eḷaka*;
the sacrificial post is the *indakhīla*. A pillar is the *thambha* or *thūṇa* (both masculine and feminine).
*Pāṭikā* refers to a wooden beam; *ḍḍhenda* and *pāsāṇa* refer to a stone; *giñjakā* refers to a brick.
*Valabhi* refers to a wooden roof-covering; *gopānasī* refers to a curved rafter.
*Viṭaṅka*, however, refers to a female dove-cot (*kapotapālikā*) and is used in the feminine gender.
The keyhole is the *tāḷa*, and the opening is the *kuñcikā*;
the door-leaf is the *āvāpuraṇa*. The railing is called the *vedikā* or *vedi*.
The assembly is the *pakkhapāsa*, and the pillars of the temple are the *tulā*.
*Thiyaṃ* means both a broom and a cleaning tool.
*Saṅkaṭīraṃ* refers to a rubbish heap, a place for refuse, or a mound of trash;
furthermore, it denotes sweepings, litter, refuse, and filth.
The site of the house and so forth is the "ground" (*vatthu*); the village is the "dwelling place" (*saṃvasatha*).
The town is well-known as the "enjoyment" (*bhoga*). Now, that which is declared [to be] superior to death and the like is called and described as "the overlord" (*adhibhū*) (Ṭīkā).
And the boundary is the limit (*mariyādā*). Now...
Ghoso, Gopālagāmako.
The Chapter on Cities is finished.
3. The Chapter on Men.
A human being, a mortal, a man, a youth, a progeny-born,
a person; a male, a man,
a son of Manu, and furthermore, a wise one.
The Buddha is wise and discerning, virtuous, possessed of insight, and skilled;
he is intelligent, of refined intellect, a poet, proficient, far-sighted, and confident.
He is sagacious, thoughtful, wise, learned, knowledgeable, and a seer.
A wise man is *dhīra*, one who knows aversion is *vipassī*, and an enlightened one is *buddha*,
*dabba*, or *vidvasu*. A woman is *itthī*, *sīmantinī*, *nārī*, *thī*, *vadhū*, *vanitā*,
*ṅganā*, *pamadā*, *sundarī*, *kantā*, *ramaṇī*, *dayitā*, or *balā*.
A woman is called *mātugāma*, *mahilā*, *lalanā*, *bhīru*, or *kāminī*;
a maiden is *kumārikā* or *kaññā*; a young woman is *yuvatī* or *taruṇī*.
A queen who has been consecrated is a *mahesī*.
A courtesan is a "woman of pleasure" (bhoginī) or a "king's woman" (rājanārī);
she who goes to an appointment is a "prostitute" (dhavatthinī), while one who carries lotus roots is a "lotus-root carrier" (bhisārikā).
A "harlot" (gaṇikā) is a "common woman" (vesiyā) or a "beautiful one" (vaṇṇā); a "slave girl" (dāsī) is a "beautifier of the city" (nagarasobhinī).
A courtesan who lives by her beauty is a *vesī*; a wanton woman is a *kulaṭā* or a *bandhakī*.
A woman of noble form is a *varārohā*, a *ttamā*, a *mattā*, a *kāsinī*, or one of excellent complexion (*varavaṇṇinī*).
A devoted wife is a *patibbatā*, a *satī*, a *kulitthī*, or a *kulapālikā*.
A widow is one whose husband is absent; a woman who seeks a husband is one who is self-restrained.
A woman who has given birth is one who has brought forth; a woman who has recently given birth is a woman in childbirth.
A female messenger is a go-between; a slave girl is a servant or a housekeeper.
Vāruṇī is a momentary [liquor], while a Kṣatriya woman is a true Kṣatriya.
Wife, spouse, and partner; mistress, consort, and beloved;
co-wife and second wife—these are the various terms for her who attends upon one’s feet.
A female friend is called *sakhī*, *ālī*, or *vayassā*; a paramour is *jārī* or *aticārinī*.
In the case of a male, however, *rajo* and *pupphaṃ* refer to the [pubic] hair; one who is in her fertile period is *utunī* or *rajassalā*.
One who possesses menses is *pupphavatī*; one with a heavy womb is *garugabbhā*; and one pregnant is *pannasattā* or *gabbhinī*.
The womb is *jalābu*; the embryo is *kalala* (masculine or neuter).
A husband is *dhava*, *sāmika*, *bhattā*, *kānta*, *pati*, *vara*, or *piya*;
furthermore, he may be called *papati*, *jāra*, or *thā*.
*Paccaṃ*, *putto*, *atrajo*, and *suto* mean son.

*Tanujo*, *tanayo*, and *sūnu* are also used for son; while *putta* and the others may refer to a daughter when used in the feminine gender, *duhitā* and *dhītā* are specifically feminine terms for daughter.
*Sajāta* means one born together; *tvo’raso* means son.

*Jāyāpatī*, *janipatī*, and *jayampatī* are synonyms for husband and wife. However, the term *dampatī*—as in the phrase *dampatī*—is a masculine plural ending, ending in the vowel *i*; thus it is *tudampati* (according to the Ṭīkā).
Furthermore, *vassavara* is said to mean a eunuch (*paṇḍaka*) and a neuter (*napuṃsaka*).
A kinsman (*bandhu*) is a relative (*sajana*), one of the same clan (*sagotta*), a blood relation (*ñāti*), or a cognate (*ñātaka*);
likewise, one who shares the same maternal lineage (*sālohita*) or the same funeral cake (*sapiṇḍa*).
But "father" (*tāta*) refers specifically to the progenitor (*janaka*).
*Amma*, *mbā*, *jananī*, and *mātā* mean mother or progenitor; *janetti* and *janikā* are also [terms for] mother.
An *upamātā* is a foster-mother, while *sālo* is a brother-in-law.
A husband’s sister is a *nanandā*; a mother’s mother is an *ayyikā*.
A mother’s brother is a *mātula*, and his wife is a *mātulānī*.
The mother of a husband and wife is called a *sassu*, and her husband is a *tappitā*.
A father-in-law is *sasura*; a nephew is *bhāgineyya*; a son is *putta*; a sister's son is *bhaginiyā putta*.
A grandson is called *nattā* or *papotta*; a husband’s brother is *sāmibhātā* or *devara*;
and a daughter’s husband is *jāmātā*.
But the *ayyaka* is the grandfather.
The mother’s sister is the maternal aunt; the father’s sister is the paternal aunt.
The great-grandfather is the *payyaka*.
A daughter-in-law is a *suṇhā*, a *suṇisā*, or a *husā*.
A brother from the same womb (*sodariya*) is one who shares the same womb (*sagabbha*), a *sodara*, or a *sahaja*.
