whereas a *heraññika* is a mint-master or coin-examiner.
The immediate neighbor is the enemy; beyond him is the friend and the king.
The non-friend, the foe, the adversary, the rival, the hater, the enemy, the foe, the adversary, the opponent, the obstacle-maker, the counter-opponent, and the one intent on harm [are synonyms].
(Enemy + Foe). The adversary, the obstacle-maker, the counter-opponent, and the one intent on harm.
Enemy, adversary, opponent, hostile, and antagonist;
foreigner, direction, seen, place, compliance, and following.
Friend, companion, fellow, associate, bosom friend, (according to the *Ṭīkā*) well-wisher, and comrade.
A relative is one with whom one has shared a meal; a firm friend is one who has been seen for a long time; a mere acquaintance is one seen only briefly.
A resident is one who lives there; a traveler is one who journeys on the earth; a wayfarer is one who has gone a great distance.
A messenger is one who carries a message; a calculator is one who works by the moment.
The scribe, the engraver, color, and also the syllable;
division, punishment, conciliation, and bribery—these are the four means (*upāya*).
Sowing discord is instigation; punishment, however, is violence and restraint.
The ally, the treasury, the difficult terrain, the victory, and the force—
these seven factors of sovereignty (rajaṅga) may also be considered as the natural constituents (pakati).
His power, his counsel, and his control are indeed the three forces (satti).
The power born of punishment is "tejo" (splendor),
while the heat born of the treasury is "patāpo" (glow).
That which is "manto" (incantation) and "mantanaṃ" (counseling) has four ears and two spheres of operation.
*Tigocara* means a group of six; *rahassa* is explained as secret.
In three senses, it refers to being secluded, uninhabited, and covered; *raho* and *rahaṃ* mean privacy.
*Vissāsa* and *vissambha* mean confidence.
What is appropriate and fitting in three respects:
exhortation, instruction, and admonition toward women—excluding men;
as well as command and teaching; this is the summary and the binding.
*Āgu* means an offense (*mantu*); *maparādho* is the same. *Karo* refers to a tax (*bali*), while *muccate* means it is released.
*Puṇṇapatto* is one who bestows satisfaction; *upadā* and *pābhataṃ* mean a gift.
Likewise, *upāyana*, *mukko*, *paṇṇākāro*, and *paheṇakaṃ* all mean a present.
*Tva* is used for a tax, while *anitthī* refers to a cluster of trees and the like. *Deyya* means a gift, *thāya* means a place, and *dhanāgama* means the acquisition of wealth.

*Ātapatta* and *chatta* both mean an umbrella. For kings, however, there is the golden seat, the lion-throne (*sīhāsana*), and likewise the fan made of hair, which is feminine, and the yak-tail whisk (*cāmara*).
The sword, the parasol, the head-ornament, the sandals, and the fly-whisk—
these five are the insignia of royalty for kings.
The auspicious jar, the full jar, the water-sprinkler, and the water-giver;
The elephant, the horse, the chariot, and the foot-soldier constitute the fourfold army.
The elephant is called a kuñjara, a vāraṇa, a hatthin, a mātaṅga, a dvirada, a gaja, a nāga,
a dvipa, an ibha, and a dantin.
The leader of the herd is the chief of the troop.
[The elephants are] Kāḷāvaka, Gaṅgeyya, Paṇḍara, Tambā, Piṅgala, Gandha,
Maṅgala, Hema, and Uposatha.
These are the six-tusked elephant clans:

the young elephant (*kalabha*), the *bhiṅka*, the rutting elephant (*pabhinna*), the intoxicated one (*matta*), the trumpeter (*gajjita*), the herd of elephants (*hatthighaṭā*), and the elephant species (*gajatā*); while the female elephant is the *kareṇukā*.
The *kumbha* is the mass of the elephant’s head; the *cūlikā* is the base of the ear.
The *āsana* is the region of the shoulders; the *mecaka* is the base of the tail.
The *ālāna*, *māḷhaka*, and *thambha* refer to the post; the *nitthī*, *nigaḷa*, and *anduka* refer to the chain and fetter.
Saṅkhalaṃ means “chain”; atho gaṇḍo means “swelling”; kaṭo means “hip”;
dānaṃ means “gift,” but [it also means] “intoxication”;
soṇḍo means “trunk” in two senses; tha means “then.”
The tip of the trunk is the *pokkhara*;
the binding at the middle is the *kacchā*; while the *kappana* refers to the goad and so forth.
An elephant fit for the king is an *opavayha*; when fully equipped, it is called *sajjita* or *kappita*.
A thorn for piercing may be at the foot of the *tomara* flagstaff;
the *tutta* is at the base of the ear, while the hook (*aṅkuśa*) is at the top of the head.
The elephant-rider is the "elephant-lord."
An elephant is *hatthi*, and its keeper is *hatthigopaka*.
A leader of the herd is *mātaṅga*; one who trains horses and so forth is *hayādyācariya*.
A horse is *hayo*, *turaṅgo*, or *turago*.
The stallion and the Sindhava horse;
the mule is its offspring,
while the jāniya is of noble breed.
The well-trained horse that carries one easily,
the young colt, the thoroughbred,
the wild stallion, the swift one, and the one exceeding in speed;
The bit is the *mukhādhāna*, while the whip is the *kasā* that strikes.
The nose-rope is the *kusā*; the hoof of the horse is the *sapha*.
The tail is not feminine [but neuter], being the *naṅguṭṭha*; the mane is the *vālahattha* and the *vāladhi*.
The chariot Sandana was for Phussa, while that of Naraṇa was Ratho;
Cammāvuta was for Veyaggha,
and Deppa for Byaggha Dīpina.
A palanquin (*śivikā*) and a litter (*yāpyayāna*); a cart (*śakaṭa*), however, is not female.
A wheel is called a component of a chariot (*rathāṅga*); its end is the rim (*nemī*), which is feminine.
In the middle of that is the hub (*piṇḍikā*), which is the nave (*nābhi*); the axle-pin, however, is the *yugandhara*.
The *akkha* is the axle-pin, the *itthi* is the axle-tree, and the *varutha* is the chariot-fender.
The *dhura* is at the front of the chariot, while the *saṅga*, *tva*, *akkha*, and *pakkhara* are its other parts.
A vehicle (*yāna*) is a means of transport (*vāhana*), a draft-animal (*yogga*), and includes all carriers such as elephants and so forth.
A chariot-rider is a *sūta*, as well as a driver and a charioteer;
a chariot-climber is a *rathika*,
while a warrior who is a soldier is a *rathī*.
*Padāti* and *patti* are feminine, while *padaga* and *padika* are considered masculine.
*Sannāha*, *kaṅkaṭa*, *vamma*, *kavaca*, and *uracchada* denote armor.
*Jālikā* and *tha* refer to one who is armored, as well as one who is ready (*sajja*) or one who is clad in mail (*vammika*).
Attached and firmly bound, a forerunner and one who goes ahead;
a leader and one who goes at the front, slow-moving and sluggish;
swift, hurried, and impetuous—one who should conquer what is to be conquered is thus liberated.
A hero, a brave one, and one who has ventured forth; a companion and a follower are synonymous.
"Equipped" and so forth apply to three [categories]; furthermore, provisions and travel gear are synonyms.
An army, a banner-bearing force, a host, a camp, a circle, and a force are likewise synonyms.
The arrangement of the divisions or the array of the army is called a *byūha*.
An elephant consists of twelve *pōsas*.
A man, a horse, and a chariot—
by this characteristic, they are called "the fourfold army" (catur-aṅginī senā).
An elephant corps, a cavalry corps, and a chariot corps— each of these three [is further divided].
The elephant-force and so forth, together with their weapons, constitute the infantry division (*pattānīka*) consisting of four types of men.
When sixty bundles of bamboo poles, each containing sixty staffs, are covered in dust by the army as it marches, that which causes agitation is called *akkhobhanī*; [it is] for the sake of stability.
*Sampatti*, *sampadā*, and *lakkhī* mean prosperity (*siri*); *vipatti* and *āpadā* mean misfortune.
Furthermore, there is also a reading of *athāvu*, *daṇḍa*, and *āyudha*; it is a weapon (*heti*) for a woman, while *sattha* and *paharaṇa* would be [the terms for] a male weapon.
*Muttāmutta* and *mamutta* refer to that which is released from a living being (*pāṇito*), and indeed, *mutta* alone [also refers to it].
"Released by a machine" refers to all weaponry, which is fourfold:
that which is released by a machine, such as a staff and so forth; that which is not released [by a machine], such as a dagger and so forth;
that which is released by the hand, such as a sword and so forth; and that which is released by a machine, such as an arrow and so forth.
*Issāsa* is an archer; *dhanu*, *kodaṇḍa*, *cāpa*, *nitthi*, and *sarāsana* are a bow;
furthermore, *guṇa*, *jiyā*, and *jyā* are a string;
and *sara*, *patti*, and *sāyaka* are an arrow.
*Vāṇa*, *kaṇḍa*, and *musu* refer to two types [of arrows]; *khurappa*, *urappa* (variant: *ka.*), and *tejanāsana*;
*tūṇī* (feminine) and *kalāpa* refer to the quiver, as do *tūṇa*, *tūṇīra*, and *vāṇadhi*.
*Pakkha* and *vāja* mean feather; *diddha*, however, refers to an arrow smeared with poison.
*Lakkha* is the target, *sara* the arrow, and *byañjana* the mark; *upāsana* is the practice with arrows.
*Maṇḍalagga*, *nettiṃsa*, *asi*, and *khagga* refer to a sword; *sāyaka* is an arrow; *kosī* is its sheath;
*tho* is its scabbard; and *tharu* is the hilt of the sword and other such weapons.
*Kheṭaka* is a shield, *phalaka* is a shield, and *camma* is leather armor; *illī* is a hand-guard (*karapālikā*).
*Churikā*, *satthī*, and *asiputtī* are knives; *laguḷo* and *muggaro* are clubs.
*Sallo* is a dart (feminine), *saṅku* is a stake (masculine), and *vāsī* is an axe (feminine).
The *kuṭhārī* and *kudhārī* (according to the commentary) are axes; the *ṭaṅka* is a stone-cutter’s chisel.
The *kaṇaya* and *bhindivāḷa* are types of slings; likewise, the *cakra*, *kunta*, and *gadā*;
and the *sattha* and so forth are varieties of weapons.
The word *koṇo* is used for the corner (*koṭi*) of a woman.
*Niyyāna*, *gamana*, *yātrā*, *paṭṭhāna*, *gama*, and *gati* all mean going or departure.
*Cuṇṇa*, *paṃsu*, *raja*, *dhūli*, *itthī*, and *reṇu*—these last two apply to both genders—mean dust.
A *māgadha* is called a honey-tongued man; a *vandī*, however, is a reciter of praises.
A *vetālika* is one who awakens [others];
a *cakkika* is a bell-ringer.
The banner, the flag, and the pennant, as well as the plantain tree as a standard—
whatever egoism there is toward one another, that would be the "I-am-first" (ahaṃmika) mentality.
Strength, power, endurance, and prowess, as well as valor and extreme heroism;
The drinking that occurs for one who has conquered in battle is considered the "victory-drink" (*jayapāna*).
Battle, combat, strife, conflict, and war;
conquest, challenge, fight, struggle, and clash—these are synonyms for battle.
Quarreling and dispute, contention, strife, and discord;
delusion, infatuation, and then stubbornness;
forceful compulsion—this is what constitutes violence.
The verse beginning with "Uppādo uppāto" (1027) should be consulted regarding a transformation of the elements (*bhūtavikati*) which indicates good or bad fortune;
*īti* refers to calamity, a woman, or the ignoble; *upasagga* means misfortune or affliction.
*Nibbuddha* and *niyuddha* refer to wrestling (*mallayuddha*); however, *vijaya* is victory.
Defeat in battle is breaking, flight, and lack of effort.
Killing, slaying, and slaughter; banishing and destruction;
harming, injury, and violence; murder, striking down, and execution.
Death, passing away, dissolution, mortality, transgression;
termination, finality, destruction, time, end, and decease—these are synonyms for death.
In three [contexts], it is called *peta* and *pareta*.
A dead man is one who has been cremated;
the funeral pyre and the cemetery are the same. A corpse is a wretched, lifeless thing.
A headless trunk is a wretched body, empty of a head yet still possessing its functions.
Now the cemetery is explained: for it is in the charnel ground among the raw corpses.
The "karamara" is the female jackal; the living being therein is clearly indicated.
"Kāra" means a prison house, while "kāraṇā" refers to torment.
Thus ends the section on Khattiyas.
A *brahmabandhu*, a *dvija*, a *vipra*, a *brahmā*, one who addresses others as "bho," a *brāhmaṇa*, a *sottiya*, and a *chandasa*— these are the terms for a Brahmin.
The pupils of Sissa are masculine.
The student of the holy life, the householder, the forest-dweller, and the monk—these four exist;
"hermitage" (*assama*) is neuter.
Practicing together with fellow celibates in virtue and the other [perfections],
the preceptor (*upajjhāya*) and the one who acts as a preceptor (*upajjhā-thā*), the teacher (*carīyo*), and the one who gives dependence (*nissayadādiko* / *nissayadāyako*).
Having first brought [the student] near and praised [him], the twice-born (*dvija*) should cause him to master the Vedas in their midst.
He who practices the tradition together with its secret lore among the brahmins is a true practitioner.
The traditional knowledge handed down through succession, as well as the instructions and ancient legends, constitute the sacrifice;
therein, the sacrificial ground is the altar, and the earth is the sacrificial bed.
The horse-sacrifice, O man, the human sacrifice, the unbarred sacrifice,
the *sammāpāsa*, and the *vājapeyya*— these are the great sacrifices.
There are the *itvijas*, the *iditvijas*, and then the *yājaka*.
A member of an assembly, a social person; likewise, *parisā*, *sabhā*, *samajjā*, *samiti*, and *saṃsad*.
There are four assemblies: monks, nuns, laymen, and [laywomen].
Regarding the term "laywoman" (upāsikā), these may be the nine assemblies:
those of the Thirty-three, the twice-born (Brahmins), the Khattiyas, Māra, and the householders;
as well as those of the ascetics, the Four Great Kings, and the Brahmās.
The meter headed by the Gāyattī, which consists of twenty-four syllables and is the foremost of the Vedas,
is the three-footed Sāvittī. Caru is considered the offering for the cooking of oblations,
while Sujā is the sacrificial grass for the burnt offering.
The finest food is pāyāsa, while the sacrificial offering is called *habya*.
This sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is a pillar carved from wood; however, in two cases it refers to the two fire-drills (*araṇī*).
The three fires are the household fire (*gāhappacca*), the offertorial fire (*āhavanīya*), and the southern fire (*dakkhiṇaggi*).
Relinquishing, giving away, generosity, renunciation, and relinquishment;
bestowing, granting, forsaking, and surrendering—
these five great abandonments of wealth are called the supreme, O Best One.
By way of one's children and wife, and likewise the constituents of a kingdom;
food, drink, a house, clothing, a vehicle, garlands,
ointments, perfumes, a bed, and a lamp— these may be the ten bases for giving.
On that very day, the gift is for the deceased; these three are for the funeral rites.
But the gift for a father is a "scattering" (nivāpa); however, in terms of its purpose, it is the same as that [gift for the deceased].
An *atithi* is a guest (*āgantu*); furthermore, a *pāhuṇa* is one who stays for a night (*vesika*).
One desiring to go elsewhere is a *gamika*; a way is a *magghiya*.
Foot-washing water and the like are *pajja*; "beings," "having come," and so forth occur in the three genders.
*Apacitya*, *accanā*, and *pūjā* mean worship; *pahāra*, *bali*, and *mānanā* mean honor.
Homage (*namassā*) is indeed *namakkāra*, as are veneration (*vandanā*) and salutation (*abhivādana*);
aspiration (*patthanā*) and resolve (*paṇidhāna*), while the latter is said to pertain to a person.
Entreaty (*ajjhesanā*), however, is honor (*sakkāra*), which is a preliminary application.
Seeking is searching, a quest, an investigation;
but attendance is the desire to hear, which constitutes service.
Silence is non-speaking, which is silence; its state is thus a sequence.
*Anukkama* is sequence; *anupubbī* is the same, while *krama* is masculine.
*Tapa*, *saṃyama*, and *sīla* are asceticism, restraint, and virtue; whereas *niyama* is a vow.
*Vītikkama* and *ajjhācāra* mean transgression; *viveka* is seclusion. *Puthuggatta* means individuality.
The minor and lesser rules are called "observances of conduct" (samācārika);
however, that which is other than those is declared to be the "virtue that is the foundation of the holy life" (ādibrahmacariya).
One who is inclined toward evil dwells together with [the consequences of] his own qualities.
One should understand him as an *upavāsa*, one who has renounced all enjoyments.
He is an ascetic (*tapassin*), a monk (*bhikkhu*), a recluse (*samaṇa*), one who has gone forth (*pabbajita*), and one whose wealth is austerity (*tapodhana*).
Furthermore, he is a sage restrained in speech (*vācaṃyama*), a silent seer (*muni*), an ascetic (*tāpasa*), and a rishi (*isī*).
Those groups of ascetics who have mastered their faculties and are self-controlled—
Sāriputta is their leader, the venerable Dhammasenāpati;
and then there is Kolita Moggallāna.
One who has reached the Noble [Path] would be [an Ariya];
those in training, such as stream-enterers and so forth, are [Ariyas], but the worldling is not an Ariya.
Furthermore, "higher knowledge" (aññā) refers to Arhatship, while a "stupa" (thūpa) would be a shrine (cetiya).
The Dhamma-treasurer Ānanda, and likewise two others;
Visākhā, Migāra’s mother, and Sudatta Anāthapiṇḍika;
a bhikkhu, a novice, a trainee, and a bhikkhunī.
She is called a *sāmaṇerī*; these five are her companions in the Dhamma.
The bowl, the three robes, the waistband, the razor, the needle, and the water-strainer—these eight requisites have been declared.
The novice (sāmaṇera), the ascetic (samaṇa), the one who teaches (adesa), and the sky-clad (digambara);
the naked (aceḷaka) and the Jain (nigaṇṭha), while the matted-hair ascetic (jaṭila) is one who wears matted locks (jaṭādhara).
The four types beginning with the kuṭīsaka, and the thirty-four [other] views, making sixty-two views in total.
Thus these ninety-six sects have been fully described.
[There are those who wear] a sacred thread, one purified by water, or one who is cleansed; likewise, one with a hide or an antelope skin;
one with a tooth-stick or a tooth-cleaner; or one wearing bark or a *tirīṭa* garment.
The vow of standing on one foot belongs to women; the water-pot is the *kuṇḍikā*.
Furthermore, regarding the support-stick (*ālambanadaṇḍa*), the *kattarayaṭṭhi* is for women.
That which is constantly dependent on the body as its means and consists of action is *yama*.
The work of a guest is impermanent; there would be a fixed rule.
Thus ends the section on Brahmins.
Then there are the *vessa* and those of *vesiyāna* birth; livelihood, occupation, and means of subsistence.
Livelihood, maintenance, and then agriculture, the male farmer,
and the female farmer; trade, the merchant, and then cattle-herding, the tending of livestock—
these are the three vocations of the *vaiśya*, the householder, the one with a home, the layperson.
A "field-liver" is a farmer; here, "field" (*khetta*) refers to a plowed plot (*kedāra*).
A "clod" (*leḍḍu*) is a lump of clay; "digger" (*khaṇitti*) means a spade.
"Sickle" (*dātta*), "reaper" (*lavitta*), and "mower" (*masita*); the word *asita* is both masculine and neuter (see verse 1005). "Goad" (*patoda*) means a whip or a driver's stick.
*Yotta* is a rope for horses and women; *phāla* is a ploughshare, while *kasaka* is a ploughman.
*Naṅgala*, *hala*, and *sīra* mean a plough; *īsā* is the shaft of the plough.
*Sammā* refers to the pin of the yoke, while *sītā* is the furrow made by the plough.
Mung beans and so forth are "other grains" (paraṇṇa), while rice and so forth are "grains" (pubbaṇṇa).
Rice, paddy, millet, wheat, varaka, barley, and kaṅgu—these are the seven types of grain;
wild rice (nīvāra) and the like are its sub-varieties.
Caṇaka is the chickpea,
and siddhattha is the mustard seed.
Then kaṅgu is the millet, piyaṅgu is the panic seed, ummā is the hemp, and atasī is the linseed.
Kiṭṭha, sassam, and dhañña are to be understood as synonyms for grain. Vīhi is rice; thambakarī and thambhakarī refer to the stalk.
Kaṇḍa is the stem, while palāla is the straw, which is fruitless.
Bhusa and kaliṅgara refer to chaff, and thusa refers to the husk of the grain.
Setaṭṭikā is a disease of the grain; kaṇo is the husk;
khalo is the threshing floor; thambo (also spelled thambho) is a cluster of grass and the like.
A pestle is neuter, while a mortar, a winnowing basket, and a measure are feminine;
furthermore, a fire-pot and a hearth are feminine, whereas a mat and a rug are masculine.
A cooking pot is feminine, while a small jar, a bowl, a trough, a shallow dish, and a large pan are masculine.
*Kolamba*, *maṇikaṃ*, *bhāṇaka*, and *arañjara*;
*Ghaṭa* (in two genders), *kuṭa* (neuter); *Kumbha*, *kalasa*, *vāraka*;
*Kaṃsa* (is) a bowl for eating; *Mattaṃ*, *patto*, and *bhājanaṃ* (are all) bowls.
*Aṇḍupaka* is a wick; *sarāva* and *mallaka* are synonyms for a bowl.
*Kaṭacchu* is masculine, while *dabbī* is feminine; *kusūla* is said to be a granary.
*Sāka* is not feminine; *ḍāka* is a leafy vegetable; *siṅgīvera* is *addaka*.
Mahosadha is dry ginger, while marica is black pepper.
Sovīra is said to be sour gruel, āranāḷa is fermented rice-water, and dhaññambila is sour gruel from grain.
Biḷaṅga is sour conjee, and lavaṇa is called salt.
Sāmudda, sindhava, nitthī, kāḷaloṇa, and ubbhida;
together with biḷaka and biḷāla—these are the five varieties of salt.
Furthermore, there are guḷa, phāṇita, khaṇḍa, macchaṇḍī, and sakkharā.
These are the products of sugarcane; then there is jaggery, which is like a poisonous thorn.
There may be parched grain, and then roasted barley; fried grains, and barley flour;
unground meal, and stirred drink; cakes, and then non-cakes, which are flour-balls.
A *bhattakāra* is a cook, as is a *sūpakāra*, a *sūda*, or an *āḷārika*; likewise, an *odanika* and a *rasaka*.
Soup (*sūpa*), however, is a condiment (*byañjana*).
Rice (*odana*) or boiled grain (*kura*) is called *bhatta*; furthermore, *bhikkhā*, *anna*, and *sana* are synonyms for food.
Food, eating, and nourishment refer to solid food,
while tarala refers to rice gruel and the like.
Edibles, chewables, lickables, and drinkables constitute the fourfold nutriment.
Nissāva is the liquid [of food], and likewise ācāma;
ālopa is what becomes a morsel (kabaḷa).
Maṇḍa refers to the essence of the juiceless [food], while vighāsa refers to the remains of what has been eaten.
The eater of remnants and the tamer; thirst and its quenching.
Hunger is appetite; the taste that covers the flesh.
Excess and belching; satisfaction and satiation.
One may indeed have as much as one desires, as much as one wishes for, and as much as is sufficient according to one's liking;
yet the merchant who buys and sells, the carrier of goods, and the trader of wares—
he is merely a seller, a peddler.
*Kāyika* refers to bodily [debt];
*uttamaṇṇo* is a creditor, while *dhamaṇṇo* is a debtor.
*Uddhāra* is said to be the debt (*iṇa*), whereas the principal (*mūla*) is the capital (*pābhata*).
*Sacca* means truth or the act of making true; *paṇiya* is that which is to be sold, in three genders.
*Paṭidāna* is an exchange; *nyāsa* is a deposit, while *upanidhi* is a pledge.
From eighteen onwards, they are called *saṅkhyeyya*; the numbers from one onwards are used in all three genders.
In reckoning both the number and the thing numbered, twenty and so forth are used for unity;
for groups, divisions, and plurality, they go up to ninety-nine.
A hundred, a thousand, a niyuta, a nahuta (or nayuta in some places), a lakh, a koti, and pakoti;
Koṭi, pakoṭi, nahuta, and likewise ninnahuta;
akkhobhani, itthi, and akkhobhiṇī (variant: bindu), abbuda, and nirabbuda;
ahaha and ababa, as well as ṭaṭa, sogandhi, and kuppala.
The *kumuda*, the *puṇḍarīka*, the *paduma*, and the *kathāna*;
then the *mahākathāna* and the *asaṅkhyeyya*; and likewise *ni’, cetāsu*, and *satādi*.
Each subsequent term is tenfold, then a hundredfold, and then a millionfold.
Four and a half is "aḍḍhuḍḍha";
likewise, three and a half is "tiyaḍḍha.
Two and a half is "aḍḍhateyya," while one and a half is "diyaḍḍha."
A second [measure] would be one and a half [times that];
then the *tulā*, the *pattha*, the *aṅguli*, and the *vasā*—thus the measures are threefold.
Four *viha* are one *guñjā*.
Two *guñjā* make one *māsaka*;
five *māsakas* make one *akkha*; eight *akkhas* make one *dharaṇa*.
Five *dharaṇas* of gold make one *nikkha*, which is not feminine.
Four *pādas* make one *bhāga*; ten *dharaṇas* make one *pala*.
A hundred *palas* make a *tulā*, and twenty such *tulās* make a *bhāra*.
Furthermore, the *kahāpaṇa* is neuter, while the *karisāpaṇa* is said to be masculine.
One kuḍuva is one pasata;
there would be four of those to make a pattha;
four patthas are an āḷhaka; and four āḷhakas are a doṇa.
Four *doṇas* make a *māṇikā*; four *māṇikās* make a female *khārī*;
twenty *khāris* make a *vāha*;
and ten *ambaṇas* may be a *kumbha*.
An āḷhaka is a finished measure, a tumba is a female measure, a pattha is a male measure,
and a nāḷi is a female measure; a vāha is a cart-load,
and ten doṇas are an ambaṇa.
*Paṭivīsa* and *koṭṭhāsa* mean a portion;
*aṃsa*, *bhāga*, and *dhana* mean wealth.
*Dabba*, *vitta*, and *sāpateyya* refer to property; *vasu* and *vibhava* have the same meaning.
Kosa, hirañña, and kata are synonyms for gold (kañcana); rūpiya refers to silver.
Kuppa denotes other [precious metals] such as copper (tamba) and the like; rūpiya is used in two senses.
Suvaṇṇa, kanaka, jātarūpa, soṇṇa, and kañcana are synonyms for gold.
Satthuvaṇṇa, harī, kambu, cāru, hema,
hāṭaka, tapaniya, hirañña, cāmīkara, sātakumbha,
jambu, nada, siṅgī, and nāriya are its varieties.
Silver (*rūpiya*) is silver (*rajata*), pure (*sajjhu*), possessed of form (*rūpī*), pure, and also wealth (*vasu*);
and the jewel (*ratana*) is the gem (*maṇi*) in two [meanings], such as the *puṣparāga* and others, which are its varieties.
Gold (*suvaṇṇa*), silver (*rajata*), pearl (*muttā*), gem (*maṇi*), and beryl (*veḷuriya*).
The diamond and coral— these beings call my seven jewels:
the ruby and the lotus, the red gem and the crimson pearl,
the bamboo-colored beryl, the coral, and the lightning-stone.
Masāragalla, kabara-maṇi, then muktā and muktikā;
rīti, rīrī (ṭī.), or ārakūṭa, while amala would be abbhaka.
Loha is neuter, ayaḥ is masculine, and kāḷā is feminine.
Mercury is the essence of silver;
lead is from kāḷatipu, while yellow orpiment is pītana.
Vermilion is cinapiṭṭha, and likewise cotton is tūla or picu.
*Khuddaja* refers to small honey; *madhucchiṭṭha* refers to beeswax.
*Gopāla* means a cowherd; *gopa* means a cow-counter.
*Gomā* and *gomika* mean an owner of cattle.
*Usabha* means a bull or a draft ox (*balibadda*); *goṇa* and *gosabha* mean a young bull, my friend.
*Vuddha* refers to an old bull; *damma* is a young steer (*vacchataro*).
*Dhuravāhī* means a beast of burden; *govinda* is one who drives cattle.
*Vaha* is a part of the shoulder (*khaṇḍha*); *kakudha* and *kakuda*—the latter is called *kaku*;
furthermore, *visāṇa* and *siṅga* mean horn. A red cow, however, is *rohiṇī*.
A cow that has horns is *gāvī* and *go*; a barren cow is called *vasā*.
A cow that has recently calved is a *navappasūtikā*; one who is fond of her calf is *vacchalā*.
A water-pot is a *gaggarī*, while two types of churns are *manthanī*. A tethering rope is called a *sandāna* or a *dāma*.
Cow dung is *gomiḷha* (masculine and neuter); furthermore, clarified butter is *sappi* and *ghataṃ*.
Navuddhaṭaṃ (unmilked), nonītaṃ (not yet churned), damimaṇḍaṃ (cream), and matthu (curdled milk);
khīraṃ (milk), duddhaṃ (milking), payo (milk), and thaññaṃ (breast-milk); takkaṃ (buttermilk) and mathitaṃ (churned).
Milk, curd, ghee, buttermilk, and nonītaṃ—these five are the products of the cow.
*Urabbha*, *meṇḍa*, and *mesa* mean ram; *uraṇo*, *avi*, and *eḷaka* also mean ram.
*Vassa*, *tvaja*, and *chagalaka* mean goat;
*oṭṭho* and *karabho* mean camel.
The donkey is called *khara*, and the ewe is *urāṇī* or *ajā*.
Thus ends the section on the Vessas.
The Śūdra is dark-complexioned and a *vasala*; the Māgadhas and others are of mixed origin.
The Māgadha is born from a Sudda father and a Kṣatriya mother; the Uggā is born from a Sudda father and a Kṣatriya mother.
The Sūta is born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Kṣatriya mother. The Kārū is one who works with tools, while the Sippika is one who works with crafts.
A Saṅghāta is a collection of those of the same birth; their group (seṇī) is said to be twofold.
The woodworker, the weaver, the dyer, the barber,
and fifthly the leather-worker— these five may be craftsmen.
The woodworker is considered a carpenter (*vaḍḍhakī*), also known as a *palagaṇḍa* or a *thapati*.
The chariot-maker, the goldsmith, and the worker in reeds;
the weaver, the tailor,
and the garland-maker as well.
The potter and the weaver,
the tailor and the needle-maker;
the leather-worker, the chariot-maker, the barber and the bath-attendant.
The dyer, the painter, the scavenger who discards flowers,
the bamboo-worker, the reed-worker— these three are equal;
the carpenter and the turner.
The smith and the metal-worker;
the dyer and the washerman, the fisherman and the water-carrier;
the lute-player and the bamboo-worker, the fletcher and the carpenter.
A bamboo-blower is a *veṇavika*;
a hand-clapperer is a *pāṇigha* or *pāṇiya* (in some places);
a cake-seller is a *pūpiya* or *pūpapaṇiya*; a tavern-keeper is a *soṇḍika*, a seller of spirituous liquor.
Māyā is the art of illusion, while Kāra is a conjurer of magical nets;
the sheep-butchers, pig-butchers, deer-hunters, and bird-catchers—
they live by killing goats, pigs, deer, and birds respectively.
A hunter is one who uses snares, while a fisherman uses nets;
a porter is one who carries loads;
a hired laborer is one who receives wages, while a servant is one who performs work for nothing.
The slave (dāsa), the servant (ceṭaka), the purchased (pessa), and the son of the master (bhacca) who serves;
the one born in the house (antojāta), the one bought with wealth (dhanakkīta), the one who has voluntarily entered into slavery (dāsabya-apagata),
and the one brought as a captive from war (karamarānīta)— thus there may be four kinds of slaves.
But he who is not a slave, being a free man,
though low-born and of humble origin,
is one who does not abandon his duty and is untiring.
But the Manda is one who is lazy and also a cook;
he is a Caṇḍāla, a Mātaṅga, and a Sapañca.
The various sub-divisions of these are the Milakkha tribes, such as the Kirātas, Savaras, and others.
A hunter, a deer-killer, a fowler;
a deer-stalker, one who hunts deer;
a dog of the breed of Śarameya, a hound, a son, a Ṣoṇa, and a kukkura.
*Svāna*, *suvāna*, and *sāḷūra* [mean dog];
*sūna*, *sāna*, and *sā* are masculine;
one who has fallen into madness and so forth is called *aḷakka*; thus *sūna* is considered [another term for] a dog.
A leather thong is a *gaddūla*, while a lamp-wick is a *cetaka*;
a knot is a binding, and a snare is a *vāgurā* or *vākarā*, used for binding deer.
A basket is a *thiyaṃ*, a *kuveṇī*, or a *kumīnaṃ*; a net is called an *ānaya*.
*Āghātanaṃ* is a place of execution; *sūnā*, however, is a slaughterhouse.
A *takkara*, a *mosaka*, and a *cora* are synonyms for a thief;
likewise, *thena*, *ekāgārika*, and *sama*.
Theft, robbery, and plundering;
*vemo* is a weaver’s loom.
*Sutta* and *tantu* (masculine) mean thread; *pottha* refers to work such as plastering.
A *pañcālikā* or *potthalikā* is an image fashioned from cloth, ivory, or other materials.
An *ugghāṭana* is a water-wheel (*ghaṭīyantra*), which is a mechanism for drawing water from a well (*kūpa*). A *mañjūsā*, *peḷā*, and *piṭaka* refer to a box or chest;
the latter two terms are also used for a small basket or hamper. When referring to a woman, the word *pacchi* denotes a small wicker basket, while *peṭaka* refers to a larger basket or bag.
A carrying-net for women is called *byābhaṅgī*; a small basket used as a sling is *sikkā*.
A sandal is *upāhana* or *pādu*, and its varieties are *pādukā*.
Leather thongs are *varattā*, *vaddhikā*, or *naddhi*; a leather bag is *bhastā* or *cammapasibbaka*.
A crucible for melting gold and so forth,
a mold, or an iron hammer;
tongs used by smiths, and a female smith’s bellows held in the fist.
A water-pot is called *gaggarī*; a ripe *pippala* fruit is called *sattaṃ*.
A coarse cloth is said to be *nikasa*;
a needle for piercing is *ārā*.
*Khara* means harsh or rough; *kakaca* means a saw; *nitthī* means a woman; *sippaṃ*, *kammaṃ*, and *kalādikam* refer to craft, work, and the arts such as those of a craftsman.
*Paṭimā* and *paṭibimbaṃ* mean an image or likeness; *bimbo* is considered a synonym for *paṭinidhi* (a counterpart).
*Samo*, *paṭibhāgo*, *sannikāso*, and *sarikkhako* are synonyms used in the sense of "equal" or "similar" among three things.
Samāna means similar, like, or equal;
saṅkāsa, sannibha, and nibha are likewise;
opamma and upamāna also mean comparison, while pamā is used specifically for women.
*Nibbesa*, *vetana*, and *mūlya* mean "stake" or "wager"; *jūta* (neuter) means "gambling.
A gambler is called a *dhutta*, *akkhadhutta*, or *kitava*; he is also a *jūtakāra* or an *akkhadevina*.
A guarantor is a *pāṭibhoga* or *paṭibhū*; an *akkha* is a gaming die (*pāsaka*).
The *puṃmēvā* is the eight-footed *aṭṭhāpada*; the *sāri* is on the board, and the *paṇa* is the stake.
What indeed is the seed of intoxication? Honey is considered *madhu*, and *madhvāsava* is honey-liquor;
*madirā* is *vāruṇī*, and *majja* is wine; *surā* is fermented liquor, while *meraya* is distilled spirit.
The words *saraka*, *caṣaka*, *nitthī*, *āpāna*, *pāna*, and *maṇḍala*—
which are used here with a broad application (*bhūrippayoga*) for each of the [four] *yogika* [categories]— should be understood as applying even to other genders,
because they possess those same properties despite having a different mode of occurrence (*aññavutti*).
Thus ends the Chapter on the Suddas.
The Chapter of Four Fifties is finished.
5. The Chapter on Forests.
Arañña, kānana, dāya, gahana, vipina, vana, aṭavī, and mahārañña—these are synonyms for forest;
however, *itthi* (woman) refers to a female ruler among kings.
That which is planted by those who are peaceful, not too far from the city, is called a grove (*ārāma*).
The grove is called *taruṣaṇḍa*, and likewise it is called a forest (*pavana*).
The wilderness (*arañña*) is common to all; when the king has departed, it is released.
That very thing should be known as negligence (*pamada*), which is long-accumulated in the forest and the mantras.
*Panti*, *vīthi*, *āvali*, and *seṇī* mean a row; *pāḷi*, *lekhā*, and *rāji* mean a line.
A tree is called *pādapa*, *viṭapī*, *rukkha*, *ago*, *sāla*, and *mahīruha*.
It is also called *duma*, *taru*, *kuja*, and *sākhī*; whereas a small tree is called a *gaccha*.
Those that bear fruit without flowers are called forest trees (*vanappati*).
That which dies at the conclusion of the ripening of its fruit is known as a *sadhī*.
In three genders, *vañcya* means "deceptive" and *aphala* means "fruitless"; *phalina*, *phalavā*, and *phalī* mean "bearing fruit.
*Samphullita* and *vikaca* mean "in full bloom," while *phulla* and *vikasita* are used in all three genders.
*Sirogga*, *sikharo*, and *nitthī* refer to the "summit" or "peak," whereas *sākhā* is said to be a "branch" or "creeper."
*Daḷa*, *palāsa*, *chadana*, *paṇṇa*, *patta*, and *chada* are synonyms for leaf.
*Pallava* or *kisalaya* refers to a young shoot; however, when it has newly sprouted, it is called *aṅkura*.
*Makula* or *kuṭumala* refers to a bud, while *khāraka* or *jālaka* refers to a new leaf-sprout.
*Kalikā* is a bud; *vaṇṭa* is the stalk that binds the flower and so forth.
*Pasava*, *kusuma*, and *puppha* mean a flower; *parāga* is the pollen born from the flower.
*Makaranda* is considered honey; *thavaka* and *gocchaka* refer to a cluster of blossoms.
In the case of *phala*, [the forms] *āmaphalam* and *salāṭuphalam* are used;
however, when the fruit is ripe, it is called *pakvaphalam*.
The names for flowers such as *campaka* and *ambāḍi* are neuter.
But *mallikā* and so forth refer to the flower; *vīhi* refers to the grain in its husk;
*jambū* is used for the fruit, while *jambu* and *jambavaṃ* refer to the tree; *viṭapa* and *viṭabhī* refer to the branch.
From the root up to the end of the branches, the trunk is considered one part of the tree.
*Koṭara* is a hollow in a tree; *cchidra* is a hole, while *kaṭṭha* and *dāru* mean wood.
*Bunda* and *mūla* are the root, while *pāda* is the base. *Saṅku* and *khāṇu* refer to a stump.
*Karahāṭa* is the bulbous root (*kanda*), while *kaḷīra* is the sprout (*matthaka*).
*Vallarī*, *mañjarī*, and *nārī* are synonyms for a creeper (*vallī*), which is also called a vine (*latā*).
A pillar (*thambha*) and a cluster (*gumba*) are not trunks (*akkhandha*); a vine is a plant with various forms that creeps along.
*Assattha* and *bodhi* are two names for the same tree; *nigrodha* is the name for the *vaṭa* (banyan) tree.
The *kaviṭṭha* and the *kapittha*, while the *udumbara* is a limb of sacrifice;
the *koviḷāra* and the *yugapatta*, the *uddāla* and the *vātaghātaka*;
the royal tree, the *katamālī*, the *nandīvāra*, and the *byādhighātaka*.
Dantasaṭha and jambhīra, varaṇa and kareri;
kiṃsuka and pālibhadda, vañjula and vetasa.
Ambāṭaka and ītanaka, madhuka and madhudduma.
Then the *guḷaphala*, the *pīlu*, the *sobhañjana*, and the *siggu*;
the *sattapaṇṇi*, the *chattapaṇṇo*, the *tinisa*, and the *timuttaka*;
the *kiṃsuka* and the *palāsa*.
Ariṭṭha is the phenila tree;
mālūra, beluva, and abilla; punnāga is the kesara;
sālava is the loddha; and piyāla is the sannakaddu.
Likocaka, likewise Aṅkola,
then Guggulu and Kosika;
Amba, Cūta, and Saha— these are they.
The *sahakāra* is fragrant;
the *puṇḍarīka* is white and yellow; the *selu* has many fruits;
the *sepaṇṇī* and *kāsmirī* are likewise; and the *kolī* and *badarī* belong to the same category.
The *kola* is not female; the *badara*, *pilakkha*, and *pippalī* are female;
the *pāṭalī* and *kaṇhavantā* are [both]; the *sādukaṇṭa* and *vikaṅkata* are [both];
the *tinduka* and *kāḷakkhandha* are [both]; and the *timbarūsaka* and *timbarū* are [both].
Erāvata, however, is the nāraṅga; kulaka is the kākatinduka.
Kadamba is the piyaka, and nīpa is the bhallī and bhallātaka in three [meanings].
Then jhāvuka is the picula, and tilaka would be the khuraka.
Ciñcā and tintiṇī, then gaddabhaṇḍa and kapītana;
sāla, assakaṇṇa, and sajjū;
then ajjuna and kakudha.
The niculo and mucalinda, the nīpa and likewise the piyaka;
the asana and the yellow sāla,
and the golīsa shall be the jhāṭala.
Khīrikā is a royal sanctuary (*rājāyatana*); *kumbhī* and *kumudikā* are synonyms. *Yūpa* and *pūga* (variant:
*kamuka*) refer to the betel nut tree; *paṭṭi* is lac-dye (*lākhāpasādana*).
*Iṅgudī* is the ascetic’s tree (*tāpasataru*); *bhujapatta*, however, is *ābhujī*.
Picchilā and simbalī refer to two [types]; rocanā is koṭasimbalī.
Pakiriya is pūtika; rohī would be rohitaka; eraṇḍa is āmaṇḍa;
then there is samī, which has seeds as its fruit.
The *nattamāla* is the *karañja* tree; the *khadira* is used for cleaning the teeth.
The *somavakka* is the *kadara*; the *sallaki* is the *madana*.
Furthermore, the *indasāla* may also be the *sallakī* or the *khāraka*.
Devadāru is bhaddadāru; campeyya is campaka.
Panasa is kaṇṭakiphala; abhayā is harītakī.
Akkha is vibhītaka in three senses; amatā is āmalakī in three senses.
The labuja, the likuca, and then the kaṇikāra, the dumuppala;
the nimba, the ariṭṭha, the pucimanda, and the karaka, the dāḷima;
the sarala, the pūtikaṭṭha, and the kapilā, the siṃsapā.
Sāma, piyaṅgu, and kaṅgu, as well as sirīsa and bhaṇḍila;
soṇaka and dīghavanta,
and vakula which has filaments.
The heartwood of the *kākodumbarikā*, the *nāga* and the *nāgamālikā*;
the *asoka*, the *vañjula*, and then the *takkārī* and the *vejayantika*;
the *tāpiñcha*, the *tamāla*, and then the *kuṭaja* and the *girimallikā*.
*Indrayava* is its fruit; *aggimantho* would be the *kaṇikā*.
*Niguṇṭhi* is the female form for *sinduvāra*; *tiṇasuñña* and *tiṇasūla*, however, are *mallikā*.
*Sephālikā* and *nīlikā* are the same; *apphoṭā* is the wild *mallikā*.
Bandhuka, jayasumana, bhaṇḍika, and bandhujīvaka;
sumanā, jātisumanā, mālatī, jāti, and vassikī;
yūthikā, māgadhī, and then sattalā and navamallikā.
Vāsantī, atimutta, karavīra, assamāraka;
mātuluṅga, bījapūra, and ummatta is mātula.
Karamanda and susena; kunda, however, is called māghya.
Devatāsa, Devatāḍa, Jīmūta, Thāmilāta, Mahāsahā,
Sereyyaka, and Dāsī.
The *kirāta* is the *kuraṇṭaka*;
the *ajjuka* is the white-flowered *paṇṇāsa*; the *samīraṇa* is the *phaṇijjaka*.
The *japā* is the *jayasumana*; the *karīra* is the *kakaca*.
Rukkhādanī and vandākā, while cittaka is designated as fire.
Akka is the scatterer therein;
you, lakkha, are the white-flowered one.
Pūtilatā, gaḷocī, mubbā, and madhurasā;
then kapikacchu, duphassa, and mañjiṭṭhā;
vikasā, ambaṭṭhā, and likewise pāṭhā, kaṭukā, and kaṭurohiṇī.
Apāmārga is the "crest-ornament," while Pippalī is considered to be Māgadhī;
Gokaṇṭaka, Siṅghāṭa, Kolavallī, and Abhapippalī [are also mentioned].
Golomī, however, is Vacā, as well as Girikaṇyā and Aparājitā.
Sīhapucchī, pañhipaṇṇī, and sālapaṇṇī are indeed firm (tu ca’tthirā); (Cathirā).
Nididdhikā, byagghī, and then nīlī and nīlinī;
jiñjuka and jiñjukā (ka.), as well as guñjā, then satamūlī and satāvarī.
Mahosadha, ativisa, bākucī, somavallikā;
dābbī, dāruhaliddā, biḷaṅga, and citrataṇḍula;
nuhī, mahānāma, and muddikā, which has a sweet taste.
Furthermore, there is madhuka, yaṭṭhi, madhukā, madhuyaṭṭhikā, and madhulaṭṭhikā;
then vātiṅgaṇa, bhaṇḍākī, vāttākī, and brahatī;
as well as nāgabalā, jhasā, lāṅgalī, and sāradī.
Rambhā is the plantain (kadalī), and moca is the cotton tree (kappāsī); badarā is the jujube tree.
Nāgalatā is betel (tambūlī), while aggijālā is the dhātakī tree.
Tivutā and tipuṭā are synonyms, as are sāmā and kāḷā.
Then there is *siṅgī* and *usabha*, while *reṇukā* is reddish-brown (*kapiḷā*).
*Hirivera* and *vāla* are [yellow], while the *bimbikā* has red fruit.
*Seleyya* and *masmapuppha* are [white], while *elā* is *bahulā*.
Leprosy (*kuṭṭha*) is declared to be a disease, while *kuṭannaṭa* is a wild herb.
"Medicine" (*osadhi*) applies to things that possess a genus (*jāti*), whereas "remedy" (*osadha*) applies to everything that lacks a genus.
Likewise, there are roots, leaves, shoots, tips, bulbs, kernels, and fruits.
The *taco-puppha* and the *chatta*— these are considered the ten kinds of potherbs (*sāka*).
The *papunnāṭa*, the *eḷagala*,
the *taṇḍuleyya*, and the *appamārisa*;
Jīvanti and jīvanī, as well as madhuraka and jīvaka;
mahākanda and garlic (lasuṇa), while palandu is sukandaka;
paṭola and tittaka, as well as bhiṅgarāja and makkava.
The *punarnavā* is a destroyer of swelling (*sotha-ghātī*); the *vitunna* is well-seated.
The *kāravello* is very fragrant; the *tumbī*, *alābu*, and *lābu* are the same.
The *eḷāluka* and *kakkārī* are similar, while the *kumbhaṇḍa* is a creeper (*vallibha*).
Indavāruṇī, visālā, vatthukaṃ, vatthuleyyaka, mūlaka, nitthiya,
cuccu, tambaka, kalambaka— these are varieties of vegetables,

One who acts without discernment should indeed be known as "fickle.

spoken, uttered, said, declared, proclaimed, muttered;

Victory, the act of conquering, and conquest;

Existence, resolve, and zeal;
likewise, fault, disadvantage, and existence;
benefit and virtue.
*Majjha*, *vemajjha*, and *muccati* are synonyms for the middle.

*Jāgaro*, *jāgariyaṃ*, and *jāgariyo* (from the Ṭīkā) mean wakefulness; whereas *pavāho* and *pavatti* mean occurrence or flow.

*yāma*, however, means restraint or self-control.

Familiarity is acquaintance;

*Lava*, *bhilāva*, and *lavana* mean "occasion";

Sannivesa and saṇṭhāna; then abbhantara and antara.

*Paṇaya* is considered [a term for] trust, entreaty, and love.
*Ṇāda* is faith (*saddhā*). *Paccaya* refers to requisites such as robes and so forth, and to conditions (*paccaya*) in the sense of causes and supports.
*Vihāra* refers to play, celestial abodes, and so forth, as well as the dwelling place of the Sugata.
"Sam" is considered to mean "in the steadfast," "citte" means "in the mind," and "samādhi" means "one-pointedness.
"Yoga" means "conjunction" and "saṅga" means "attachment" (to sensual desires).
"Jhāna" refers to "application" in the sense of being fit for the lower realms.
*Bhoga* refers to the expanded hood of a snake, crookedness, eating, and wealth;
*aṅgaṇa* is used for a plot of ground, defilement, and dirt.
*Abhimāna* is considered to mean pride regarding wealth and the like, as well as wisdom in that context.
*Apadesa* is considered to refer to a sign, a deception, and a statement;
it refers to the mind, the body, and intrinsic nature, as well as to the self (*atta*) and the supreme self (*paramat-tani*).
Furthermore, *gumbo* refers to a cluster, a pillar, and a multitude or an army.
*Niyyāsa* refers to a granary, a storehouse, a barn,
or even the interior of the belly. *Niyyūha* refers to a flight of stairs,
a crest-jewel, a crown, a turban, a spout, a gate, or a bracket.
Furthermore, *sikhaṇḍa* refers to a quiver, while *kalāpa* is considered a cluster or mass.
*Cūḷā* refers to bound-up hair, and *moḷi* refers to both a crown and a crest.
*Saṅkha* is a conch-shell, not feminine; it denotes a shell, the frontal bone, and the bones of the forehead (*lalāṭaṭṭhi*). *Gopphaka* refers to the ankle.
*Pakkha* means "side" when referring to time or strength, but it means "wing" in the context of birds. *Sakhi* refers to a friend, while *vāja* refers to horses or sacrificial offerings.
*Paṅgula* means "lame. *Sindhu* refers to a region or a river; it is masculine when denoting a river, but feminine when denoting a woman.
*Hatthi* refers to an elephant or its trunk when masculine, but it refers to a female elephant (*kareṇu*) or a woman when feminine. *Mittha* refers to a friend.
*Ratana* (jewel) is feminine when it refers to a diamond, but masculine when it refers to a gem, a thunderbolt, or a cause.
*Visāṇa* (horn) occurs in three genders: in the case of an elephant’s tusk, in the case of a beast’s horn, and in the sense of a corner or edge.
Similarly, *koṇa* (corner/edge) is considered masculine when referring to a musical instrument or its playing.
*Vaṇippatha* refers to trade routes and cities; *nigama* refers to the Vedas and towns.
*Adhikaraṇa* may mean dispute, a legal case, a support, or a cause. *Go* refers to cattle and the earth;
*go* [in the sense of speech] refers to speech; *pum* to a male, and *itthi* to a female.
*Harita* means gold; *vāsudeva* is called *hari* and *irita*.
*Āyatta* refers to attendants and retinue; *parigraha* refers to a wife.
*Uttamsa* and *avataṃsa* refer to ear-ornaments and crests.
*Vijju* means lightning; *vajira* means thunderbolt; *sani* means both woman and man;
*koṇa* means corner and a specific number; *ukkaṃsa* means excellence; *koṭi* means the tip of a woman's hair;
*cūḷā* means crest, net, chief, or top; and *sikhā* refers to a peacock’s crest.
*Ruci* is used for "a woman," "desire for what is wished for," "melted fat in oil," and "being under the sway" of others, such as barren women or snakes. However,
it is also used for "longing," "a ray of light," "attachment," and "liking" in a woman.
The term *saññā* is seen in the sense of perceiving (*sañjānana*), and also in the sense of volition (*cetanā*).
It refers to a part, a craft, a digit, a time, a portion, and the sixteenth phase of the moon.
*Kaṇṇikā* refers to the seed-vessel, the pinnacle of a house, and an ear-ornament.
In the future, in the long duration, and in its manifestation, it is considered "āyati.
*Uṇṇā* refers to the hair of the head and other body hairs, while *romadhātu* refers to the hair in the middle of the body.
*Vāruṇī* is said to refer to a woman, as well as to an actress, wine, and so forth.
*Kriyā* is used for action (*karana*), activity, and work (*kamma*);
*vadhū* is considered to mean a daughter-in-law, a maiden, and a wife.
*Matta* refers to measure, sovereignty, and a small portion of a syllable.
*Sutta* means "scripture" in the Pāli canon (*pāvacana*), "established" (*siddha*) according to the *Ṭīkā*, and "thread" (*taṃta*) or "well-slept" (*supita*) in three senses.
*Kakuda* refers to the marks of a king (*rājaliṅga*), to non-defeat (*asabhaṅga*), to a tree, and also to the plant *kakudha*.
*Byañjana* means "sign" (*nimitta*), "syllable" (*akkhara*), or "soup" (*sūpa*); it also means "condiment" (*cihna*) or "word" (*pada*).
In common parlance, *micchā* refers to gambling, as well as to playing with dice;
however, in the context of a wife, it refers to the field, while in the context of the body, it is said to mean a plot of land.
Furthermore, *issā* should be understood as service or obedience, and *upāsana* as practice or cultivation.
*Sūla* means a spit for roasting meat, a spear, a stake, a bolt, or a disease.
*Tanti* refers to the strings of a lute; *tantaṃ* means a thread, a primary tenet, or a fiber.
*Yuga* denotes the pole of a chariot and so forth; it also means an eon or a pair.
The word *itthi* refers to a flower and pollen; *raja* refers to dust and natural qualities;
*nyāsa* refers to entrusting and giving; and *niyyātana* is said to mean returning. *Garu* refers to heavy things and states of misery;
*tittha* refers to a ford and pure water; and *diṭṭhi* refers to views.
*Paṇḍaka* refers to a eunuch, a lunar mansion, or the radiance in a flame.
*Kaṇḍa* means an arrow, a reed, a staff, a class, or an occasion.
*Porisa* signifies the height of both arms raised, the measure of both arms, or heroism.
*Uṭṭhānaṃ* is used in the sense of rising up, exertion, sitting down, ascending,
and also in the sense of an independent portion of land or saline soil.
*Ārādhanaṃ* is used in the sense of accomplishing, gaining, trusting, and pleasing.
*Sānu* refers to a mountain ridge; *siṅga* is used for a horn.
*Ñāṇa* (knowledge) is the eye on the path of vision; *dassana* (seeing) refers to the attainment of moments.
*Nikkha* is used for five gold pieces and for an ornament in the feminine.
In the division of lunar days it is a branch and so forth; in a fruit, a joint is released.
