Furthermore, *apakaraṇe* means accomplishment; *sādhanaṃ* refers to the instruments among the agents.
*Tīsvīrito* and *tīsvito* (from the Ṭīkā) refer to giving and virtue; *vadaññū* means one who speaks charmingly.
*Purakkhato* refers to one who is consecrated, and *pūjite* to one who is honored and placed in front.
*Manda* occurs in one devoid of fortune, in one who is stingy, deluded, or incompetent;
it occurs in the sense of "exalted" when applied to growth or to one who is arrogant.
*Akka* refers to the axle of a chariot, gold, dice, and the sense-faculties (*indriya*).
*Sassate* (eternal) and *dhuve* (in the three [worlds]) mean permanent; *dhuvam* (certainly) and *take* (in a conjecture) mean decided.
*Hare* means Śiva; *sivam* means auspicious (*bhadda*); in the sense of liberation (*mokkhesu*), it is *jambuke*;
*sivā* refers to a female jackal. *Balam* occurs in the sense of an army, a spear, and stoutness.

The number eight (*aṭṭha*) occurs in the classification of hells, in the lotus among water-born flowers, in the classification of deities, as a masculine noun, in the sense of a eunuch, a jewel, and wealth.
It may also denote *nibbāna*, the attainment of the goal, and liberation (*apavagga*). The letter *tha* [is used for these meanings].
*Puṇḍarīka* means a white lotus in *setambuja* (a white water-lily), and a male tiger in *rukkhantara* (among trees).
*Bali* is masculine when it means an offering, and it is also masculine when it refers to the hand or a class of deities (*āsura*).
*Sukka*, however, means "origin" (*sambhave*) and "white"; in the sense of "wholesome," it is used in all three genders.
*Dāya* means "to give" (*dāne*) or "to be divided" (*vibhattabba*); it refers to wealth, the forest-wealth of one's fathers (*dhane ca pitūnaṃ vane dhane*; Ṭī.).
*Pabhutta* means "dependence" (*āyattatā*) or "independence" (*anāyatta*); it denotes mastery (*vaso*) over objects of desire (*abhilāsesu*).
*Paribhāsana* means "reproaching" (*makkose*), while *bhāsane* [is used] in the sense of "restriction" (*niyame*) and "speaking" (*tha ca*).
The word *seḷana* occurs in the sense of wealth; *sīhanāda* is seen in the sense of a lion’s roar.
*Pabhava* occurs in the sense of origin, cause, source, place, and initial perception;
furthermore, *atho* occurs in the sense of "then" and in the two months beginning with Hemanta among the flowers of the year.
*Karaṇaṃ* means the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*); *kriyā* refers to the sense-faculties within the limbs.
*Tātaḥ* means a drumstick (*tāḷa*) or a key; *tūriyaṅgaṃ* means a musical instrument or a tree.
*Pasavo* refers to flowers and fruits; *uppādo* refers to birth or the delivery of a fetus.
*Gāyana* means singing; *gāyaka* means a singer; *assa* means a horse; *gandhabba* refers to a class of deities.
*Vinā* means a lute; *vanappati* refers to a tree that bears fruit without flowers;
*rūpiya* refers to wrought gold and silver, as well as to unworked silver.
*Pāsa* refers to a snare for binding birds and the like; *kesa* refers to hair and also to a heap;
*tārā* refers to the pupil of the eye and to a constellation; *tāra* refers to a high-pitched sound.
*Kaṃsa* refers to a type of metal vessel and to four *kāhāpaṇa* coins.
*Majjhima* refers to the middle of the body, the intermediate state of existence (*antarābhava*), and the third [of the three] meditations.
*Āvesana* refers to a workshop, a possession by a spirit, a craft-hall, and houses.
*Sobhā* refers to beauty, success, and prosperity. *Sirī* refers to a mark, a woman, and a deity.
*Kumāra* refers to a crown prince, as well as to *khaṇḍa*, *susu*, and *sumi*;
furthermore, it denotes a non-feminine [gem], coral, a type of jewel, and likewise a sprout.
*Paṇa* is considered to mean wages, roots, trade, and wealth.
*Paṭiggaha*, however, is said to mean "receiving" (*gahaṇa*) and also "a vessel" (*bhājana*).
It is further stated to mean "the foul" (*asubha*), "the beautiful" (*subha*), and "karma" (*kamma*); thus it is used in two senses.
*Pipphala* refers to a species of tree and also to a needle for cutting cloth.
*Apavagga* means relinquishment, liberation at the end [of existence],
the characteristic mark in the genitals, and the defining feature of masculinity and so forth.
*Sagga* means generosity, intrinsic nature, creation, meditation, and heaven.
*Rohita* refers to a red fish, as well as a species of deer.
*Niṭṭhā* means accomplishment or completion, as well as the end or conclusion; it also implies invisibility.
*Kaṇṭaka* refers to an enemy, a thorn on a tree, or horripilation.
*Mukhya* is used for means, for the face, and in the sense of "first.
*Dabba* is used for what is possible, for a vessel that serves as a support for virtues, for wealth, and for woods known to the wise.
*Māna* is said to mean measure, a standard, and pride.
Furthermore, *parissama* is used in the sense of fatigue, while *vāyāma* and *vīriya* both mean exertion.
*Saroruha* and *satapatta* refer to a lotus; *satapatta* also refers to a bird.
*Chidda* and *chiddavanta* mean a hole or an aperture, while *susira* refers to a hollow within a musical instrument.
When there is one [word] that is similar, it is considered to have the same gender as its referent (*vācya-liṅgika*);
furthermore, *saṃvega* is understood in the senses of reverence, fear, and agitation.
*Juṇhā* refers both to the light of the moon and to the night endowed with that light.
A celestial mansion in the abode of the deities, and a seven-storied house;
the month of Jeṭṭha, the three Buddhas—these are the three praised ones.
And the Dhamma is the best among auspicious things; it is the most excellent among these three praised things.
*Gaha* means the sun and so forth in the sense of "seizing," as well as a bond and a house.
*Kāca*, however, refers to a kind of clay, a carrying-net, and a disease of the eyes.
*Gāmaṇi* has three meanings: it denotes an excellent person, a lord, and the eldest of a village.
*Bimba* refers to a reflection, a disk, or the fruit of the *bimbī* tree.
*Bhājana* and so forth refer to requisites, while *bhaṇḍa* refers to merchandise or even capital wealth.
*Magga*, however, refers to a hurried path, the factors beginning with right view, or a road.
He is equal in years, equal in weariness, and equal toward the three peaceful ones;
he has cast away confidence, O archer, in the archer and the one who shoots.
A fool is [reckoned] by the three stages of life and so forth, as well as by his association with the unwise.
*Rattaṃ* means blood; *tambā*, *nuratta*, and *rañjite* in three genders.
*Tanvī* refers to skin and body in the feminine; in three genders it means sparse, thin, or emaciated.
*Sisiro* refers to a change in season; it means snow or cold in three genders.
*Sakkhara* is seen in the sense of a kind of sugar-candy, and also in that of gravel;
however, it is considered to mean a favor or a brief summary. *Saṅgaha* is understood as grasping or inclusion.
*Paṭu* refers to one who is clever, sharp, skillful, free from disease, or proficient.
*Rāja* is used for a Kṣatriya, a lord of men, and a master.
*Khala* refers to a threshing floor, a low person, and may also mean "dust" or "powder.
*Athu* means arising, a collection, and also a condition. *Samudaya* means a multitude and also a causal condition.
*Brahmacārī* [is used] for a householder and so forth; *assama* [refers to] a hermitage in a forest of asceticism.
*Bhayaṅkara* means terrible; *kaṭhina* means harsh. *Kurūra* is used in three senses: cruel and merciless.
*Kaniṭṭha* and *kaniya* are used in three senses; furthermore, *atyappa* is used for one who is young.
*Sīgha* means quickly or light; *iṭṭha* means desired; *nissāra* means devoid of essence;
*agaru* means in threads or sutures. *Adhara* means below; it is used in three senses: inferior, a lip, and also a tooth.
*Sussūsā* means the desire to hear and service.
*Hattha* is seen in the sense of "hand" (*pāṇi*), "jewel" (*ratana*), "within a herd" (*gaṇa*), "inside a trunk" (*soṇḍā*),
"in a pit" (*āvāṭa*), "in a well" (*udapāna*), "in a well" (*kūpa*), and "in a pot" (*kumbha*).
*Āda* is used first in the sense of "beginning" (*padhāna*) and "foremost" (*pamukha*), and it possesses all three genders.
*Vajja* (fault) is of three genders when detailed: it is feminine in *vajjabhede*, neuter in *vita*, and masculine in *taṃ*.
*Sāra* (essence) is of three genders: it is masculine in *sāro*, neuter in *bale*, and masculine in *thiraṃse*; it is also used for the "highest" (*uttame*).
*Bhāra* (burden), however, refers to the burden of the aggregates (*khandhabhāra*) and so forth, and also to two thousand *palas*.
*Mandira* refers to a temple and a type of disease; *khaya* refers to destruction and decline.
*Vāḷa*, however, denotes a beast of prey and a snake; it is used in three genders for "cruel.
*Sāla* refers to the *sajja* tree and a tree in general; *sālā* is seen in the sense of a house.
*Sota* is said [to mean] hearing, sacrifice, and also listening.
*Pata* (in the three genders) means beyond, overcome, dead, and born in the realm of the departed (*petayoni*).
*Patīta*, which changes its gender according to the noun it qualifies, means known, joyful, and understood.
*Ādhippāya* means intention (*adhippāya*) and support (*ādhāra*); *āsaya* is explained as both these and abode (*thāna*).
*Patta* means wing (*pakka*) and leaf (*dala*); *patto* [is used] for a bowl (*bhājana*), and it has three meanings when referring to what has gone (*gata*).
*Sukata* means well-done (*sukata*); it is used in three senses: for that which is well-made and for the act of doing well.
“O ascetic, out of compassion, you have been addressed in private, O rich in austerity.
[The term] *surādilola* applies to three [senses]; *soṇḍa* applies to two, namely the trunk of an elephant;
*assādane* applies to the tongue, and *rasana* applies to both the tongue and the wealthy man.”
*Paṇīta* means sweet in three ways, or also excellent when prepared;
it refers to the main street, a row, a path, a woman, evil, the sky, suffering, misfortune, and sin (*agha*). *Muccati* [is used] in these senses.
*Paṭala* refers to a collection, a film on the eye, a disease, or a covering.
*Sandhi* is used for a joint or connection, and it also exists in the sense of rebirth (*paṭisandhi*).
The seventh [vowel] among the seven is the best for completing [the meter]; it occurs in the third, seventh, and third [syllables].
*Oja* (vital essence) is used for sustaining life, for radiance, and for strength;
furthermore, it is said to mean "observing" as well as "seeing" and "hearing.
*Gabbha* refers to a being dwelling in the womb and to the womb itself, as well as to inner apartments.
*Khaṇḍana* means cutting off, as well as a deed (*apadāna*) and what has been said (*itivutta*). *Kammaṇi* refers to actions.
*Cittaka* refers to a type of tree and a mole (*tilaka*), while *tilakāḷaka* refers to a dark mole.
*Sīlāda* refers to practice (*paṭipatti*) and a woman (*itthī*). *Patti* refers to enlightenment (*bodhi*) and occurrences (*pavatti*).
In the phrase *asumhi āyuṃhi*, see verse 407 (*Ṭīkā*). In the sense of "living being," it refers to breath, sentient beings, and the heart-wind.
In the sense of "will," it refers to inclination, intention, the Vedas, desire, and the *anuṭṭhubha* meter, etc.
In the sense of "flood," it refers to a collection, the surge of a flood, and the current of water.
*Kapāla* refers to the bone of the head, as well as to entire objects such as jars.
*Jaṭā* refers to a network of bamboo branches and the like, as well as to matted hair and a dwelling place.
*Saraṇa*, however, means killing, a house, that which is protected, and the act of protecting.
*Thiyaṃ* is used in the sense of "beloved," "dear," "lovely," and "charming," and it possesses three genders.
*Gavakkha*, however, means "window" and "collection"; *jāla* means "net" and "the binding of fish and so forth.
*Kiṃ* is used in the sense of "question," "reproach," and "restriction," and it possesses three genders.
*Sasaddhe* occurs in three senses: as a *nivāpa* (sacrificial offering), as *saddha* (faith), and as *saddhā* (the act of faith) when it functions as a condition (*paccaya*).
*Bījaṃ* is seen in the sense of a cause (*hetu*), in the number eight (*aṭṭhi*), and in the sense of the generative organ (*aṅgajāta*).
*Pubba* occurs in the sense of pus (*pūya*), at the beginning (*agga*), and at the front (*agga*)—[according to the Ṭīkā]—or at the start (*ādi*).
Thus, from the perspective of direction, it possesses three genders.
In the case of the fruit and the mind, it is the "cause" (hetu); in the case of gain and grain and so forth, it is the "fruit" (phala).
In the case of coming, however, it is "long" (dīgha) and so on; and in the Nikāyas, it is "scripture" (āgama).
*Santāna* is said to mean a divine tree, as well as continuity (*santati*).
*Anuttara* occurs in three senses: in the sense of superior (*uttara*) and its opposite, and in the sense of supreme (*seṭṭha*).
*Vikkama* is said to denote capability (*satti*) and excellence (*sampatti*), as well as mere beauty (*kantimatta*).
*Chāyā* refers to the absence of sunlight, to a reflection, and to radiance.
*Gimha*, *ghamma*, and *nidāgha* denote heat; furthermore, they refer to sweat.
*Kappana* is said to mean cutting, as well as imagining, optionality, and acquisition.
*Anga* means "much" when referring to a limb (*aṅga*), and *aṅga* means "body" when referring to a part (*vapumha’aṅga*)—so too in the sense of "parts" and "causes.
*Devālaya* refers to a temple, and *thūpa* refers to a stupa; *cetiya* refers to a shrine, and *cetiya’duma* refers to a sacred tree.
*Sajjana* refers to a virtuous person, and *sajjanaṃ* is used in the sense of "preparing" (*kappane*). Furthermore:
The word *supina* [is used] in the sense of sleep and in the sense of consciousness;
it is feminine. *Sannidhi* is described as being present and in close proximity;
it occurs further in the sense of abundance, and in another sense it is an indeclinable (*abyaya*).
*Visālitta-sare* means smeared on a wet surface; *diddha* is smeared on what is already dry;
*tiliṅgika* refers to the three genders. *Vāsa* refers to perfumes and such preparations;
*dhivāsa* refers to acceptance. The word *visārado* is used in three senses: for one who is confident, for one who is very bold, and for a wise person.
Now, *sittha* is said to mean beeswax; *vutta* is said to mean that which arises from boiled rice.
*Kasāya* refers to a liquid, a color, a variety of taste, and something fragrant.
Furthermore, *uggamana* is said to mean arising, as well as birth and upward movement.
The word *lūkha* refers to harshness; *pharusa* refers to that which has the characteristic of being spoken harshly;
*pavāha*, however, is seen in the sense of a flow and in the sense of occurrence (*pavatti*). The term *parāyaṇa* occurs in three senses:
as a support, as one who is intent upon, and as what is desired.
*Kavaca* refers to armor or a coat of mail, as does *vāra-vāṇa*; *nimmoka* and *kañcuka* refer to a snake’s slough or a bodice.
*Tamba* is considered a type of metal, namely copper; when meaning "red," it has three genders.
In the sense of "known" or "understood," it is used in all three genders; in the sense of "concluded" or "reaching the end," it is considered neuter.
In the sense of awakening and giving, *paṭipādana* is to be understood;
in the sense of a rock and a place free from water, it refers to deities and is uttered as *marū*.
*Sattha* refers to weapons and treatises; *sattha* also refers to a caravan and a collection.
*Vutti* is used in the sense of livelihood, opening, conduct, and woman.
*Parakkama* is said to mean energy and heroism.
Furthermore, *kambu* is considered to mean conch, gold, and a bracelet.
*Saro* occurs in the sense of a reed, a sound, or a pond, and is feminine;
*kharo* occurs in the sense of roughness, sharpness, or a donkey, and is used in three genders;
*āsavo* occurs in the sense of liquor, a calamity, sensual pleasures, and that which possesses a taste.
*Upadhi* means "body" or "chariot-part"; it also means "substratum" in the sense of the four bases (*upadhi*).
*Vatthu* means "site," "cause," "substance," or "type of earth"; it refers to the Three Jewels (*ratana-ttaya*).
*Yakkha* refers to a deity, a Great King, a follower of Kuvera, or a human being.
In a block of wood, on a stool, in a shop, on a chair or seat;
in an entourage, as equipment, as materials, and as adornment.
In trade, in setting aside, and in the designation of what exists.
*Paṭibhāna* refers to wisdom (*paññā*) and to speech that has been mastered.
*Hetu* is stated in the sense of a constituent part of speech and its root; it also means cause (*kāraṇa*).
*Pācā*, however, means the stomach (*udara*); *gahaṇī* means the small intestine (*nalasmiṃ*) in the sense of "that which seizes."
*Piya* means "beloved" when referring to a husband, a wife, or a lover; it has three meanings when meaning "desired.
*Yama*, however, refers to the King of Death (*Yamarāja*) in the dual number, and also signifies self-restraint.
*Madhu-rita* refers to the juice of the *muddika* flower and to something small.
*Ulloca* is used for the expanse of the sky, while *vitāna*—which may be masculine or neuter—is used for a canopy.
*Amata* is considered to mean liberation (*apavagga*), water, and nectar (*sudhā*);
however, *tama*—which is not feminine—is used for delusion (*moha*), darkness (*timira*), and as a numeral or a quality (*guṇa*).
In *khara*, *akāriye*, and *tīsu*; in *rasamhi* and *purise*; in *kaṭu*;
in *paṇḍake*, *sukate*, *puññaṃ*, *manuññe*, and *pavane*—in these three [each];
*rukkho* in *dumamhi*; in *pharusā*; and in those three *siniddhesu*.
*Uppatti* is used for cause, origin, and semen.
*Sambhava* is used for origin, a sign, a cause, the male organ, and a mark.
*Ādi* is considered to mean boundary, assistance, vicinity, and a part.
In the Vedas, "manta" means counsel; through wisdom, one is released from counsel;
it is seen in misfortune and calamity, as well as in failure.
*Aruṇa* refers to the breaking of rays and to a deep red color.
The prefix *anu-* signifies "natural state" (*pakatā*), while *ni-* is used for "returning" and "disappearance.
*Ava-* occurs in the sense of "entering," as well as in "landing-place" (*tittha*), "opening," and "gap.
Furthermore, the letter *ā* is said to denote "cause," as well as "shape" and "gesture."
*Suddi* refers to a son and a steward; *ugga* is used in three senses:
intense, a high official (*mahāmatta*), and one who is naturally superior or resolute.
*Kalla* means at dawn, healthy, or skilled in preparation and dexterity—this applies to all three [meanings]. *Tīsu taṃ*: that [term] is used in these three ways.
*Kuhanā* refers to hypocrisy (*kūṭacariyā*); *kuhana* occurs in three senses: the act of hypocrisy and the hypocrite.
*Kapota* refers to a species of bird and is seen [used] for the pigeon (*pārāvata*). *Sārada* refers to autumn and to one born in autumn;
it is used in three senses, including "one who has not yet conceived" (*apagabbha*). *Mata* means dead and is used in three senses.
In the three harsh and rigid [qualities], it is *kakkasa*; *sāhasappiya* means "beloved by violence" (*sāhasa-appiya*, according to the commentary);
in the sense of a non-act (*akāriya*), it refers to a private part of the body; *cīra* is used for a loincloth;
in the classification of animals, it refers to a banner; and *moce* refers to the plantain tree (*kadali*).
*Dakkhiṇā* is used in the sense of a gift or offering; *vāmata* means "from the left," while *dakkhiṇo* means "right.
*Dutiyā* refers to a wife, and it is considered to mean "completing" two [of a pair].
*Athuppāde* may mean "smoke," as well as "banner" (*ketu*) and "Vessānara" (Agni).
In the sense of departing from existence, it is a vehicle; at the gate, it may be an exit.
In the sense of a pilot, it refers to one who steers a ship;
it possesses three genders as a controller. Furthermore, *nirodha* signifies liberation (*apavarga*) and destruction (*vināśa*), as well as obstruction (*rodhana*).
*Bhaya* (fear) is said to be fearful; it has three genders when used in the sense of that which causes fear.
*Piṭaka* is said to mean a vessel, and likewise a scripture.
*Vali* is understood to refer to the folds of skin on the belly that become loose due to old age.
*Bhinna* is used in the sense of split, torn apart, or dependent, and it takes the gender of the word it qualifies.
*Upajāpa* is considered a synonym for *bheda* (sowing dissension), as well as for distinction and rending.
*Maṇḍala* refers to a cluster of villages, a physical form, or the circumference of a sword.
*Āṇā* means command; *āgama* means scripture; *lekha* means writing; *sāsana* means the teaching;
*anusāsana* means instruction. *Agga*, however, means peak or summit; *ayo* means piercing through illusion or a thorn; *guṇukkaṃsa* means excellence of virtues;
and *vibhava* means prosperity as well as accomplishment. *Sampatti* means success and *sampadā* means attainment.
Regarding *khamo* in three senses: "Patient toward those who are hungry, capable, beneficial, and fit" (see verse 1001).
Regarding *addho*: it occurs in the sense of a portion, a path, and time; furthermore, *addho* is an indeclinable used in the sense of "one-sided.
Moreover, *karīsaṃ* is said in the sense of excrement; it is used in four senses.
*Usabha* means bull, ox, or best (*seṭṭha*) [according to the Ṭīkā]; *sū* refers to the twenty-sixth [vowel] *u*; *usabhaṃ* is established as the object.
*Setu* is used for a bridge, a row, or a line; *pāḷi* is said to mean a woman.
*Kaṭa* means victory, a sign of possession, or a mat made of reeds; it is used in three ways when constructed.
*Mahi* is said to mean the earth, or the site of a temple and its courtyard.
*Vitakka* refers to deliberation; likewise, *takka* is considered to mean a needle’s point.
*Sudassana* refers to the city of Sakka; it is difficult to see in three ways: [as the world, as a needle-point, and as the city].
*Āloka* (light) is used for an island, a shore, a lamp, and for support and Nibbāna;
*baddha* (bound) for that which is dependent on it; *seta* (white) for the three [types of] smiles;
*thiya* (wife) for a spouse; *brahme māre sure* for a male.
*Kaṇha* [is used] for Vāsudeva and Antaka; *asita* [is used] for three [meanings]: evil, dark, and unbound.
*Upacāra* [is used] for attendance, vicinity, proximity, and planting another.
*Sakka* [is used] for Indra, a district, and the Sākiyans; *khama* [is used] for three [meanings].
*Vajjana* means exemption, protection from honor, and guarding;
*ariya* refers to the noble ones among the three [stages] beginning with the stream-enterer, and to a twice-born male;
*susuka* refers to a crocodile, a young one, and a female serpent.
*Indīvara* is considered to mean "blue" (*nīla*); *ppala* refers to the *uddāla* tree.
*Asana* means "pleasing" (*piyaka*) or a "thorn" (*kaṇḍa*); *sana* means "eating" (*bhakkhaṇa*) or "throwing" (*khipana*).
*Dhura* [is used] in the sense of a yoke (*yuga*), authority (*adhikāra*), modification (*vikāra*), effort (*vīriya*), exertion (*padhāna*), and proximity (*antika*).
*Kāḷa* is used in the sense of "three" when referring to food; *asita* is masculine in the sense of "cut.
*Pavāraṇā* is spoken of in the sense of "invitation," "refusal," and "request.
*Ummāra* refers to a door-post and a pillar; *indakhīla* is considered to mean "threshold."
*Potthaka* refers to a coarse cloth, while *gantha* refers to works such as plastering and other crafts.
*Dhañña* is said to mean rice and other grains; it is used in three senses: the grain itself, one who possesses merit (*puññavat*), and wealth.
*Pāṇi* means the hand, and *bhū* refers to living beings; it is considered to mean that which is to be made smooth.
*Pīta* (yellow) refers to the three [colors] with the luster of turmeric; it may also refer to one who is joyful or to something that has been drunk.
*Byūha* (array) is considered to mean a formation, a street, a diversion, or a troop.
*Rāga* (red) refers to the color red and so forth, as well as greed; it is also considered to mean passion or the act of coloring.
*Padara* refers to a wooden plank and its breaking; *pavuddha* refers to a crocodile.
*Siṅghāṭaka* refers to the fruit of the kaseru plant;
*maggasamāgama* (the meeting of roads) and *bahulā* (the full moon day) refer to saliva. *Eḷā* refers to cardamom; *eḷa* is explained as a fault (*dosa*).
*Ādhāra* means a support or receptacle, as in *pattādhāra* (a bowl-rest) or *lavālaka* (a basin);
*kāra* refers to a type of elephant or honor; *kārā*, however, denotes a prison.
*Karakā* refers to a rain cloud or a stone; *karaka* also refers to a water-pot (*kuṇḍikā*).
*Pāpaṇe* refers to a shop; *padātismiṃ* means on foot; *patti* refers to a woman walking.
*Chiddaṃ*, *randhaṃ*, and *vivaraṃ* refer to a hole, a cavity, or a flaw.
*Muttā* refers to a pearl; *muttaṃ* refers to urine or that which has been released (in three genders).
*Vāraṇa* means prohibition; *vāraṇo* refers to an elephant among elephants;
*dāna* means giving, abandonment, purity, cutting, lopping, and destruction;
*nibbuti* means mental satisfaction, Nibbāna, and the state of being extinguished.
*Negama* refers to one born in a town (*nigama*), as well as one who lives by trade (*apaṇa*).
*Harita* means green; *paṇṇa* means a leaf. *Palāsa* is used for the *kiṃsuka* tree.
*Pakāsa* is known in the sense of being manifest or evident; *āloka* is considered masculine.
*Pakka* means ripe fruit; it is neuter (*nāsu*) when it refers to that which has matured in the three [genders].
*Piṇḍa* is considered to mean a lump, sustenance, the body, and a ball. *Vaṭṭa* refers to a cycle of existence, wages, and a snake;
it is masculine (*so*) when it means round. It is used in all three genders (*tisu*).
*Paṭihāra* means a warder-off at a meal, and a gatekeeper at a gate.
*Bhīru* is said to mean a woman; it is used for a timid man and possesses all three genders.
*Vikaṭa* refers to excrement, urine, and the like; *vikaṭa* [as an adjective] is used in the three genders for that which is disgusting.
*Vāma* means "left" (*sabya*) and "charming" (*cāru*); *viparīta* refers to the three opposites.
*Lakṣa* is used for a numerical distinction, a target (*sarabya*), and a mark (*cihna*).
*Seṇī* refers to women of the same craft, a group, and also a row.
Sudhā means lime; dhūli is dust; cuṇṇa is powder, and vāsacuṇṇaka is scented powder.
Regarding "jetabbe" and "atippasatthe," it is said that "jeyyaṃ" refers to the three [stages] of an elder.
As for takka, it is buttermilk.
*Lolita* occurs in three genders;
*abbhuta* and *acchariya* occur in three genders, while *paṇa* and *abbhuta* are masculine;
*mecaka* refers to the base of a tail and also means "black" in three genders.
*Vasavattī* refers to Māra in the masculine, and to one who possesses power in all three genders.
*Sambhava* means impurity in the masculine, and is seen in all three genders when meaning filth.
*Accha* is said to be singular in the masculine, and is used in all three genders when meaning clear.
*Baḷisa* refers to a stone for splitting [wood]; *vaṅka* means crooked in three genders.
*Chava* is to be known as a corpse; it is used in the sense of a contemptible person and possesses all three genders.
In all three genders, it may be used in its entirety; in the masculine, it occurs in the sense of "half.

Furthermore, *candaggāha* and so forth are used in the sense of occurrence (*uppatti*), as well as in the sense of "eclipsing" (*padussana*) and "malice" (*padosa*), as stated in the introduction to the *Saṃvarī*.
*Lohita* is said to mean blood; when meaning red, it is used in three genders.
*Muddhā* is masculine when meaning the head; *muddha* is used in three genders when meaning deluded.
*Vijita* is said to mean a kingdom; when meaning conquered, it is used in three genders.
*Paritta* is used in the sense of protection (*parittāṇa*), while *paritta* also means "small" in three senses.
*Kumbhaṇḍa* is seen as a type of deity and in a species of creeper.
*Pāda* refers to a fourth part of a verse, a foot, a border, a mountain, and a ray of light.
*Vaṅga* refers to tin among metals; it denotes a country, a male person, or a plurality;
it also refers to a particular type of smith’s tool, a small measure, and a fist—these last two being dual in number.
*Ambaṇa* means a wooden trough (*doṇī*), and it also refers to a measure equal to ten *doṇas*.
*Adhiṭṭhiti* is used in the sense of a support or a basis; *adhiṭṭhāna* is said to mean a place.
*Mahesī* refers to a Great Sage (*sugata*) when masculine, and is considered to refer to a queen or a noble woman when feminine.
*Upasagga* is seen in the sense of a calamity, and also in the sense of foot-ornaments.
*Vakka* refers to a division of parts in the sense of "kidney," and it is used in three genders in the sense of "crooked.
*Vijjā* refers to sacred knowledge (*veda*), craft (*sippa*), and the like;

*tivijjā* and so forth refer to wisdom (*buddhi*). *Ekagga* is masculine when meaning "concentration" (*samādhi*), and it is of common gender (*vāccaliṅgika*) when meaning "not distracted" (*anākula*).
*Pajja* occurs in three genders: in the sense of a verse (*siloka*), it is masculine; in the sense of half [a verse], it is neuter;

and in the sense of a foot [of a verse], it is feminine. *Kataka* occurs in three genders: in the sense of a specific tree, it is masculine; in the sense of fame, it is neuter. *Assava* occurs in three genders in the sense of being obedient; *pubba* may be masculine in the sense of a person.

The word *kalyāṇa* is used in the sense of "spoken" (*kathita*) and "security" (*khema*); it is also stated in the sense of "protection" (*rakkhaṇa*) regarding the three [refuges], and in the sense of "application" (*niyojana*) and "purpose" (*payojana*) regarding what is to be done.
The word *assattha* is used in the sense of "consolation" (*assāsa*) regarding the three [refuges], and as a masculine noun, it refers to the Bodhi tree.
*Tīsu* means "in three" and *luddo* means "cruel"; it may also refer to a hunter (*nesāda*) when masculine.
*Vilaggo* means "clinging" in three genders, but it is seen as masculine in the sense of "middle.
*Aḍḍho*, however, is feminine when meaning "a portion," but is of variable gender when meaning "wealthy."
"Kaṭṭha" means wood; "taṃ" (it) refers to that which is difficult; it occurs in three senses: dense, ploughed, and with its own continuity;
it also refers to an object and a sphere of activity; "ajjhatta" means released within.
Thus ends the section on words with multiple meanings.
*Bhuva* means "in the world" and *jana* means "people"; *loka* means "fire" and *so* means "flame";
*siloka* means "fame" and *pajja* means "lineage";
*rukkha* means "tree" and *dhava* means "owner."
Nigrodha among the *vaṭa* trees, Dhaṅka among the vultures, and Vāra among the cranes;
Avasarā among the elephants, Kucetvabbha among the clouds,
Aṅka on the lap and on a mark, Rasmi among women, Juti among rays, and Rajju among ropes.
*Āloka* refers to light in the sense of being seen;
*Buddha*, however, refers to the wise Conqueror (*jina*).
*Sūra* means hero among men, as well as the sun; *daṇḍa* refers to a club, as well as punishment.
*Animisa* refers to gods and fish; *pattha* refers to desire and the *mānasa* crane.
*Ātaṅka* refers to affliction and fever;
*mātaṅga* refers to a winged elephant.
*Miga* (deer), *pasu* (beast), and *kuruṅga* (antelope); *ulūka* (owl) and *indu* (moon); *kosika* (owl-hawk).
*Viggaha* (strife) is used for quarrel and body; *purisa* (man) for youth and soul;
*dāyāda* (heir) for kinsmen and sons; *sira* (head) for the skull and lead.
*Balihattha* means hand; *dvija* refers to a Brahmin, a tooth, or a bird;
*vatta* refers to conduct, lineage, mouth, or behavior; *kaṇa* refers to a grain, a minute particle, or a flaw;
*thambha* refers to a pillar, a post, or dullness; *sūpa* refers to gruel or a condiment.
*Gaṇḍa* means a cheek (*phoṭe*) and *kapolamhi*; *aggha* means price (*mūlye*) and worship (*pūjane*).
*Pakāra* refers to equality (*tulya*) and division (*bhedesu*); *sakunta* refers to the bhāsa bird and other winged creatures (*bhāsapakkhisu*).
*Vidhi* refers to fortune (*bhāgye*) and procedure (*vidhāne*); *sāyaka* refers to an arrow (*sare*) and a sword (*khagge*).
*Sāraṅga* means a chataka bird or a deer; *pattī* refers to arrows or birds; *seda* occurs in the sense of sweat or ripening;
*vipāka* stands for maturation;
and *gaṇa* denotes a division among monks or a collection.
*Puñja* and *rāsi* mean a heap, such as a pile of sheep and so forth;
*assa* and *loṇa* mean salt from Sindh;
*saṃvaṭṭa*, *palaya*, and *nāsa* mean destruction; and *pūga* means a betel-nut, a crowd, or a heap.
*Amata* means nectar or plaster; *abhikhyā* means fame or splendor;
*sakti* means power or capability; *mahī* means a river or the earth;
*līlā* means action or graceful charm.
*Pajā* means offspring;
*upaladdhi* refers to knowledge and gain; *paveṇī* refers to bamboo and lineage;
*pavatti*, *vutti*, and *vattā* refer to occurrence, livelihood, and one who conducts affairs; *bharaṇa* means maintenance, while *bhati* means wages.
*Ācāra* means conduct or propriety; *bhūti* refers to beings or prosperity; *samiddhi* means success. *Soppa* means sleep;
*pamāda* means negligence; *tandi* means sloth. *Yātrā* refers to maintenance, going, or livelihood.
*Nindā* means blame, censure, or reproach. *Kaṅgu* refers to a type of grain or millet; *piyaṅgu* refers to the plant or its seeds.
*Sameti* means "emancipation" (*mokkha*), "peace" (*santi*), "division" (*vibhāga*), "devotion" (*bhatti*), and "service" (*sevane*).
*Icchā* means "desire," *juti* means "splendor," and *kānti* means "beauty. *Rañjane* means "pleasing," and *rati* means "delight" and "heroism" (*sūrate*).
*Vasati* means "house" (*gehe*) and "dwelling" (*vāse*). *Vāhinī* means "river" and "army" (*senā*).
*Naḷī* refers to a wooden trough, a hollow reed, a group, an assembly, or a gathering;
*taṇhā* refers to greed or thirst; *vattanī* refers to a path or a way of proceeding;
*nābhi* refers to a part of a living being or the hub of a wheel; and *viññatti* refers to a request or making known.
*Vitti* means satisfaction; *vedanā* means feeling; *ṭhāna* means in a place, while *jīvita* means stability.
*Taraṅga* means a wave; *antara* means interval; *vīci* means a ripple. *Dhīratā* means courage; *dhāraṇā* means holding; *dhiti* means firmness.
*Bhū* refers to the earth and the ground; *bhamuka* refers to the eyebrow. *Sadda* means sound; *veda* means the Vedas; *sava* means all; *suti* means hearing.
*Gotta* refers to name and lineage, as well as to city, town, and house;
*oka* refers to a support, a home, and a family; *kula* refers to lineage and the head of a clan.
*Hema* refers to wealth and gold; *paññāṇa* refers to a mark and prosperity.
Furthermore: *ambara* means sky or clothing; *guyha* means the private parts or a secret;
*tapa* means religious duty or a vow; *pāpa* means sin or a transgression;
*ratana* means a jewel or the most excellent things; and *vassa* means a year or the rainy season.
*Vana* means forest or wilderness; *vārī* means milk, water, or fluid; *payas* means milk or water;
*akkhara* means a letter or script, or liberation (*mokkha*); *methuna* means sexual intercourse or union;
*sota* means the ear or a current of water; *riṭṭha* means evil or the unwholesome (*asu*).
*Āgu* is used for sins and offenses; *ketu*, *cihna*, and *dhaja* for a banner or sign.
*Gopura* refers to a gate or even a city-gate; *mandira* means a city or a house.
From this point on, the genders are subject to change according to usage. *Byatta*, however, means a wise person or one who is proficient.
*Vallabha* means "beloved" when used with *dayitā*; *thūla* means "large" even when referring to great water;
*bhīma* refers to the "cruel" or "terrible";
whereas *lola* denotes one who is "greedy" or "fickle."
*Bībhaccha* is used for the deformed and the terrifying; *komala* for the tender and *tikhina* for the sharp;
*iṭṭha* for the desired and *madhura* for the sweet; *sādu* is used for the savory and *madhura* for that which is pleasant.
*Sita* means white and pure, while *dvijivha* refers to a double-tongued snake or a slanderer.
Sakka is capable in connection; it is fully completed in its entirety.
Suddha (pure) is among the purified and kevala (absolute); jighañña (to be sought) is among the lowest and adhama (base).
Poṇa (inclined) is toward the low-lying and apanata (bent); añña (other) is among the inferior and the rest.
*Suci* means pure, clean, white, and purified; *pesala* refers to those who are skillful and beautiful.
*Adhamo* means base or contemptible; *kucchite* means inferior or deficient. *Appiye* means unpleasant;
*pya’liko* (piyāluko) means one who is dear. *Byāpe* means impure; *saṃkiṇṇo* means mixed. *Bhabbaṃ* means capable; *yogye* and *bhāvini* mean fit and likely.
*Sukhuma* means "minute" or "subtle"; *appaka* means "small"; *vuḍḍha* means "grown old"; and *thera* means "elder" or "wise.
*Subha* means "auspicious" or "good"; *sādhu* means "virtuous"; *bhadda* means "blessed" or "fortunate"; and *tha* (in this context) refers to those [preceding]. *Vipula* means "vast" or "abundant";

*bahu* means "much. *Dhīra* means "wise"; *budha* means "learned"; and *dhitimanta* means "possessing fortitude. *Vellita* means "crooked"; *kuṭila* means "wicked"; and *dhuta* means "shaken off" or "purified."
*Visada* means wise or skilled; *seta* means white. *Taruna* refers to one who is young or fresh.
*Yogga* means fit for a vehicle; *khama* means capable or suitable.
*Piṇḍita* means counted or dense.
*Budha* means born into a noble family; *vuddha* means grown old or aged;
*kalyāṇa* means beautiful as well; *hima* means cold; *lole* means quick or fickle;
*vutta* means spoken or uttered; and *udita* means arisen or emerged.
*Āditta* means inflamed; *gabbhita* means pregnant; *ditto* means intoxicated; *piṭṭhaṃ* means flour; *cuṇṇita* means powdered.
*Vigata* means departed; *vāyita* means woven; *vītaṃ* is the same; *bhāvitaṃ* means cultivated or increased.
*Bhajjita* means fried; *patita* means fallen; *bhaṭṭho* means fallen; *puṭṭho* means asked or nourished.
*Jāta* is used for a collection of beings (*bhūte caye*) and for what is born (*jātam*);
*paṭibhāga* is used for equals (*samā*) and enemies (*arisu*);
*sūra* is used for a hero (*vīre*), the sun (*ravī*), and a hero in battle (*sūre*); *duṭṭha* is used for one who is angry (*kuddhe*) and one who is corrupted (*dūsite*).
*Diṭṭho* is used in the sense of "seen" (*arimhi*), "shown" (*ikkhite*), and "a view" (*diṭṭhaṃ*).
*Mūḷhe* means "in delusion"; *pote* means "in a boat"; and *bāliso* means "a fool.
*Nindāyaṃ* means "in blame"; *khepane* means "in causing to fall"; and *khepo* means "falling. *Niyamo* means "restriction," "certainty," and "vow."
Kusa is for a tally-stick and dabba for grass;
bālya refers to childhood and khaya to destruction;
alepa means plastering and avalepa anointing; aṇḍaja refers to fish and birds.
*Bilāla* refers to a cat or a mongoose; *mantha* to churning or the ingredients for churning;
*vāla* to hair or the mane of a horse and so forth;
and *saṅghāta* to a blow or a heap.
*Gopa* means a village; *gāma*. *Rava* means sound; *ghosa*. *Sūta* refers to those who attend upon a charioteer (*sārathi*).
*Mālya* refers to flowers and their garlands. *Vāha* refers to a cart and a horse.
*Khaya*, *accaya*, and *apacaya* refer to time (*kāla*) and the occasion (*samaya*) for the death of mortals.
The word *bha* [is used] for the pupils of the eyes, boundaries, limits, and fixed positions;
*ābhoga* for fullness, faults, and enjoyment;
*svā* for a woman, a female friend, and embankments.
*Sattha* means "sharp"; *thūla*, "gross"; *daḷha*, "firm," in three senses; *latā*, "creeper," in the sense of a branch or a climbing vine.
*Muttī*, "liberation," occurs in the senses of releasing and emancipation (*mokkha*).
*Kāya*, however, refers to the body, a collection, or a heap.

*Sikhā* (tuft), *piñcha* (feather), *sikhaṇḍa* (crest); *satte* (beings), *attani* (in the self), *puggala* (person);
*sambādha* (confined), *saṅkaṭe* (narrow), *guyhe* (secret).
*Na* is used for destruction and throwing away;
*pa* for defeat; *va* for excrement, form, and dung; *tha* for splendor, woman, and radiance;
*la* for what is obtainable, what is to be gained, and the yoke; and *kha*, *ṇḍa*, *pa*, *ṇṇa*, and *da* are considered to mean "leaf."

The particle *ca* is used for conjunction, comparison, doubt, and as a word-filler (*padapūraṇa*).
The particle *vā* is used for restricted option (*vavatthitavibhāsā*), emphasis (*āvassagga*), alternative (*vikappana*), ornamentation (*bhūsana*), prohibition (*vāraṇa*), and mastery (*pariyatti*).
The particle *alaṃ* is said to mean "enough" or "sufficient."
*Atha*, *atho*, *atha*, *anantara*, and *ārambha* [are used]; in questions and for completing a line (*padapūraṇa*).
*Pasaṃsā* and *garahā* signify praise and blame respectively; *sī* and *kārādo* also mean acceptance (*svīkāra*) [according to the Ṭīkā].
*Tha* is used in the sense of certainty and in inference (*anumāna*); *siyā* and *nūna* are used in reflection (*vitakkana*).
*Puccha* (question), *avadhāraṇa* (emphasis), *anuññā* (permission); *sāntvanā* (consolation), *ālapanē* (addressing), *santanālapane* (addressing with affection) [variant: *nanu* (interrogative)];
*vate* (exclamation), *ekaṃsa* (certainty), *dayā* (compassion), *hāsa* (laughter), *kheda* (weariness), *ālapanē* (addressing), *vimhaye* (astonishment).
*Vākyārambha* (commencement of a sentence), *visādesu* (in dejection); *handa* is used for laughter and compassion.
*Tāva* signifies totality, measure, or limitation.
*Pācī*, *pura*, and *puratthā* denote what has gone before, what is prior, or the first;
they also signify continuity and the distant past. *Purā* denotes proximity and the future.
The particle *khalu* is used for prohibition, as an ornament of speech, for emphasis,
and for establishing a proof; when placed near *abhitaḥ*, it means "on both sides," and when near *abhimukhaḥ*, it means "facing in two directions."
The particle *kāmaṃ* is seen in the sense of "willingly" (*yadyapi*), in the sense of "certainly" (*ekamsa*),
and likewise in the sense of "distinction" (*visesa*) as well as for the purpose of completing a metrical foot (*padapūraṇa*).

*Hi* is used in the sense of "cause" (*kāraṇa*), in the sense of "distinction" (*visesa*), in the sense of "holding fast" (*dhāraṇa*), and for the purpose of completing a metrical foot (*padapūraṇa*).
*Tu* is used for "cause" (*hetu*) and "therein" (*tatra*); *ku* for "evil" (*pāpa*) and "blame" (*akutsane*).
*Nu* is used for "doubt" (*saṃśaya*) and "question" (*praśna*); *tha* for "various" (*nānā*) and "separately" (*anekatva*), as well as for "avoiding" (*vajjane*).
*Kiṃ* is used for "interrogation" (*pṛcchā*) and "disgust" (*jigucchā*); *kaṃ* is used for "water" (*vāri*) and "on the head" (*mūrdhani*).
*Amā* is used in the sense of "near" (*sahassamīpe*), while *tha* is used for "division" (*bhede*) and "not first" (*appaṭhame*).
*Kiṃ* is used for "what? (*anussava*), "dislike" (*aruci*), and "even" (*udāpi*) in the sense of possibility (*vikappane*).
*Patīcī* means "last" (*carime*) and "afterwards" (*pacchā*). *Sāmi* is used in the sense of "lord" (*tvaddhe*) and "disgust" (*jigucchane*).
One should use *pātu* when revealing a possibility, but *raho* and *mitho* for things done in secret between one another.
Use *hā* in cases of exhaustion, grief, and suffering; *tva’ha* in exhaustion; and *ahaha* in astonishment.
*Bhiṃsāpana* and *hiṃsāpana* (according to the Ṭīkā); *dhī* and *dhi* (according to the Kaṇḍa) signify censure;
*pidhāne* (in the sense of covering); *tiriyaṃ* and *tiro*. *Tuna*, *tvāna*, *tave*, *tvā*, *tuṃ*;
*dhā*, *so*, *thā*, *kkhattu*, and also *meva*; *to*, *tha*, *tra*, *hiñcanaṃ*, *hiṃhaṃ*, *dhi*, *ha*, *hi*, *dha*, *dhunā*, *rahi*.
Now, *dājja*, *thaṃ*, *tattaṃ*, *jja*, *jjhu*, *ādayo*;
the compound *abyayībhāva* and the substitution of *yā*—
these become indeclinables (*abyaya*).
Thus ends the section on indeclinables.
The third chapter, on common nouns, is concluded.
The *Abhidhānappadīpikā* is complete.
The section on heaven, the section on earth, and likewise the section on common nouns—
endowed with these three sections is this *Abhidhānappadīpikā*.
In the heavens, on earth, and in the abode of the serpents,
this island is called the Fulfiller of All Aims;
the wise man who is skilled in this [is truly a person].
He was proficient in the words of the Great Sage.
A ruler of the earth named Parakkamabhuja, adorned with virtues,
was the radiant lord of Laṅkā, victorious and possessing the prowess of a lion.
For a long time he caused the divided Bhikkhu-saṅgha to be properly united within the three Nikāyas;
with constant care, as if it were his own body, for a long duration.
He protected [the island] with costly requisites;
by means of which Laṅkā was filled with monasteries, villages, groves,
and cities, crowded as if with fame itself, along with fields and reservoirs.
Having obtained his unique favor, which grants all desires,
I too have attained the status of a book-author, a domain for the wise. In the palace built by him,
adorned with gate-towers and other ornaments, [I composed this].
In the monastery known as Mahājetavana, which is highly esteemed by the virtuous and situated amidst a cluster of villages, he dwelt with a peaceful conduct,
like one who has descended from heaven and is reflected in his own waters.
This *Abhidhānappadīpikā* was composed by the wise Elder Moggallāna, who desired the endurance of the true Dhamma.
